content.title: Democracy under attack – how do we protect society's digital nervous system?
content.description: Democracies are eroded when their digital infrastructures fall outside democratic control. Three threats reinforce one another: market-driven institutional breakdown as infrastructure is privatised; authoritarian control as the state centralises digital systems; and loss of digital sovereignty.
content.extendedDescription:
Democracies risk erosion when critical digital infrastructures fall outside democratic control. Three interconnected threats reinforce one another: market-driven institutional breakdown as core data, identities and essential infrastructure are privatised; authoritarian technocratic control as the state centralises digital systems without sufficient transparency and accountability; and loss of sovereignty through dependence on clouds, platforms and AI under foreign jurisdiction.

The seminar explores how these forces make rule-making, the exercise of public authority, public access to information, archives and crisis preparedness vulnerable to manipulation, unclear responsibility and reduced legitimacy. We discuss how digital infrastructures can be designed to resist manipulation, remain resilient and allow decisions to be reversed, while strengthening democracy amid growing geopolitical and technological uncertainty.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Biochar: too good to need a national policy?
content.description: Biochar is both a physical product and a carbon sink. It is made from domestic materials, increasing the value of our biological resources. Biochar improves soils and concrete and purifies water. Carbon in soil and building materials is overlooked as a means of achieving negative emissions.
content.extendedDescription:
Biochar is an established but still underused solution for long-term carbon storage. The technology can contribute to healthier soils, climate-neutral concrete, new value chains and better use of existing energy infrastructure.

Yet Sweden lacks a national policy with clear instruments and incentives to scale up production and use. This seminar discusses how biochar can become an integral part of climate action, both as a carbon sink and as a material with practical benefits for agriculture, construction and public spaces. What policy changes are needed to unlock its potential? How can municipalities, agriculture and industry cooperate to create robust regional cycles? Researchers, practitioners and decision-makers explore barriers, opportunities and concrete next steps. The seminar consists of a short introductory lecture followed by audience questions.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: From war to a sustainable labour market — unions, migration and investment in Ukraine
content.description: How can Ukraine build a functioning and fair labour market during and after the war?
content.extendedDescription:
What roles do trade unions, labour mobility and investment play in Ukraine's reconstruction and closer ties with the EU? During the seminar, Union to Union presents a new report on the importance of unions in reconstruction, with concrete recommendations for politics and business. The discussion focuses on how dialogue and cooperation between the social partners can contribute to stability, fair working conditions and long-term development, taking the Swedish model as its starting point.
Migration is central: millions of Ukrainians have left the country amid labour shortages, while new migration flows into Ukraine are emerging, including from Central Asia. The seminar explores the effects on the labour market and the political and institutional responses needed. Perspectives from unions, politics and business are presented, focusing on Sweden's role and how international support can strengthen institutions and enable sustainable investment in Ukraine.

content.title: Leadership on the Front Line – Governing a Region Under War
content.description: How do you lead a region on the front line, partly occupied, under constant attack and hosting Europe’s largest nuclear power plant? How do civilian and military leaders cooperate to protect people, services, and stability in such conditions?
content.extendedDescription:
What does it mean to lead a region under constant threat, where parts of the territory are occupied, where civilians live under repeated attacks, and where Europe’s largest nuclear power plant remains at the center of global security concerns?
In this session, the regional leader of Zaporizhzhia will share first-hand insights into governing under wartime conditions. The discussion will address the challenges of maintaining public services, supporting civilians, and making critical decisions while operating close to an active front line.
The conversation will also include military representatives responsible for defending the region. Together, we will explore how civilian leadership and military command work in parallel, how responsibilities are coordinated, and what this cooperation looks like in practice.
This session offers a unique perspective on resilience, crisis leadership, and the reality of managing a European region in the midst of war.

content.title: One country, one electricity price – is it time?
content.description: Electricity prices affect both competitiveness and daily life, and Sweden's fragmented prices undermine acceptance of the energy transition. What is needed for Sweden to have a single common price?

Welcome to a conversation about achieving one country, one electricity price.

content.title: Why a centre for men's health is needed
content.description: Women rate their health more poorly than men do. Could one explanation be that the men around them seek too little help, consume too much alcohol and die by suicide more often than women? Some diseases are specific to men but are insufficiently detected by healthcare.
content.extendedDescription:
By following Australia's example of a publicly funded centre for men's health, Sweden could also improve its broad approach to men's health. This ranges from earlier detection of treatable diseases such as cancer and cardiovascular disease to involving both partners in sexological problems and treating fertility problems.

We want to discuss how men and healthcare can take more responsibility for men's health, and how this would benefit society as a whole.

content.title: Time for safe care
content.description: Patients should receive timely care, and care should be safe for both patients and staff. Yet this is far from guaranteed today. Staff shortages caused by poor working conditions and heavy workloads lead to waiting lists that put both patient safety and healthcare staff's working environment at risk.
content.extendedDescription:
At the same time, effective solutions exist that need wider uptake.

In this seminar, Vårdförbundet brings together political representatives to discuss how to create sustainable, safe and accessible healthcare. Starting from voters' perspectives, we discuss the most urgent challenges and what politicians need to prioritise during the next parliamentary term to make healthcare work for those who need it most and those working in it.

The discussion focuses on real-world examples: solutions that have already shortened waiting times, improved working environments and increased patient safety. What is needed to spread them and make them the norm nationwide? And what political decisions are needed to give healthcare the right conditions?

Join a seminar shifting the focus from problems to possible ways forward — for time in care and for safe care.

content.title: Being a Social Democrat in Danderyd: a challenge
content.description: Sweden's smallest local Social Democratic party organisation is in Danderyd. We have persuaded just over nine per cent of residents to vote for our alternative vision for our municipality's development. Low taxes and high quality: does that work in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Jenny Åkervall, Olle Johansson and Karsten Inde are three leading Social Democrats in Danderyd. Jenny is the leader of Socialdemokraterna's group on the municipal council, Olle is new to Danderyd but has previously served, among other roles, as a municipal executive councillor in Norrköping, and Karsten is a prominent figure in sports and community associations.

Jenny, Olle and Karsten discuss with our moderator what it means to work in a traditionally centre-right context and address challenges in schools, preschool, culture and leisure, and the housing shortage. Unfortunately, Danderyd's young people lead the statistics for alcohol, tobacco and drug use. We believe Danderyd must invest much more in prevention and in strengthening schools, culture, leisure and care for older residents.

Annika Fehling opens our meeting. Annika sings Sonja Åkesson's poems. Sonja Åkesson was born 100 years ago in Buttle on Gotland. She was a strong voice for women's right to participate in society as the welfare state was being built.

content.title: What is needed for establishment jobs to reach their full potential?
content.description: So far, few people have obtained an establishment job, leading to some criticism of the reform. What is the criticism about? And what is needed for establishment jobs to fulfil their potential?
content.extendedDescription:
Establishment jobs resulted from an agreement signed in 2022 by the social partners Svenskt Näringsliv, LO and Unionen. The system came into use on 1 January 2024. An establishment job is a special form of full-time, fixed-term employment governed by a collective agreement. It targets both newly arrived immigrants and people who have been unemployed for a long time. Employment is limited to a maximum of two years, after which it should normally become permanent. Employees in establishment jobs must be given the opportunity to take part in education during working hours without a pay deduction.

So far, few people have obtained an establishment job. The government has therefore tasked Arbetsförmedlingen with raising awareness of the scheme among employers, jobseekers and other stakeholders, with the aim of increasing the number of jobseekers employed through it. Arbetsförmedlingen and the social partners are now working together to raise awareness and improve matching so that more employers hire newly arrived immigrants and people who have been unemployed for a long time.

content.title: The foundation of Sweden's economy: efficient transport for basic and export industries
content.description: Sweden's basic and export industries are the backbone of its economy. Delivery times are critical for many companies. Today, transporting goods by rail takes export companies increasingly longer than it did 20 years ago, affecting their competitiveness.
content.extendedDescription:
Europakorridoren commissioned interviews with Swedish export companies to understand how they perceive today's transport system and how they believe infrastructure needs to develop to better meet business needs. Half the interviews were with companies based in northern Sweden. The geographical range extends from Norrbotten to Småland.

The findings show that every interviewee believes shortcomings in rail infrastructure hamper their operations. The interview results are presented at the seminar, followed by a panel discussion on the consequences and what needs to be done to strengthen Sweden as an export nation.

content.title: When the tone becomes harsher – does democracy work in digital debate?
content.description: Digital debate has become harsher. Civil society employees now face personal attacks, threats and invasions of privacy in digital channels – often anonymous and without boundaries. What does this mean for the working environment, willingness to join the debate and, ultimately, democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
Digital debate has changed. In associations, trade unions, interest organisations and other parts of civil society, employees now face an increasingly harsh tone in digital channels: hostile language, personal attacks, invasions of privacy and daily life in which the boundary between work and private life is blurred. Sometimes this is anonymous, sometimes not. Sometimes there is an underlying agenda, sometimes not.

But what does this really mean for the working environment? For well-being? For the working environment? For willingness to keep participating in public debate? And what needs to be done so that those sustaining democratic debate can do their jobs without being worn down?

Join a discussion about democratic debate. Taking the working environment as our starting point, we highlight experiences of civil society employees working in digital channels every day, and of public figures encountering an increasingly harsh tone in emails, comment sections and social media.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Family centres: the key to parenting support and violence prevention
content.description: Family centres promote good parenting and prevent violence against children. How do staff view their conditions for violence prevention work under a new Social Services Act and expanded home-visiting programmes? How can employees' knowledge of violence against children be strengthened?
content.extendedDescription:
Since 2024, Barnafrid, the national knowledge centre on violence against children, has been tasked with supporting knowledge development in family centres. The seminar presents results from the 2026 survey, in which staff reflect on their conditions for carrying out violence prevention work.

A new workplace training programme tailored to family centre staff will also be presented. The training takes place on site and is led by a facilitator from the team's own workforce.
Barnafrid provides fact sheets, facilitator materials, presentation resources and practical case vignettes: a shared, dialogue-based approach to teaching that meets staff's wishes for high-quality learning within their teams. Launch is expected this autumn.

Barnafrid briefly describes the training and this year's survey. This is followed by a panel discussion with representatives of the board of Föreningen För Familjecentralers Främjande (FFFF).

content.title: Electricity shortages and growing uncertainty — can combined heat and power deliver on both fronts?
content.description: Sweden needs more fossil-free electricity for households and businesses. In a deteriorating security environment, we also need to strengthen preparedness and secure electricity supplies to our cities in crisis or war. Could combined heat and power be the answer?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden needs more fossil-free electricity and capacity here and now. New nuclear power will take time to become available. A deteriorating security environment means Sweden must strengthen preparedness and secure electricity supply in crisis and war.

Combined heat and power already plays an important role as reserve capacity and a preparedness resource. It is weather-independent and provides balancing capability. It also has unique capabilities such as black start and island operation, which can enable local electricity supply without the national transmission grid. If our transmission grid is sabotaged, combined heat and power alone can supply our cities with electricity for several months, allowing society to continue functioning. There is also considerable potential both to increase capacity and to strengthen preparedness.

What is needed from policymakers to make this happen? Sveriges Ingenjörer, E.On, Kraftringen and Stockholm Exergi jointly invite you to a seminar seeking answers.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Can shops fine thieves?
content.description: High-volume crime and shop theft are serious societal problems. Police have long struggled to prioritise these offences, and most cases are closed when reported. Could fines following the Dutch model be a way to address the issue?
content.extendedDescription:
Watch the broadcast at
https://www.youtube.com/@livsmedelshandlarna1826

It is important to look at countries facing situations similar to Sweden's to learn and find innovative ways to address retail crime.

The Netherlands stands out as a country that has found new ways to handle retail crime more effectively while relieving pressure on police. By delegating much of the police work to shop owners, making offenders bear part of the costs and coordinating the handling of shop access bans, it has developed new ways to reduce shop theft and shoplifting.

In connection with the seminar, Livsmedelshandlarna will release a report describing the issue.

content.title: A social contract for young people
content.description: The social contract is broken. Unemployment is among the EU's highest and hits young people particularly hard. At the same time, impunity for high-volume crime is perceived to be increasing. Young people do not receive psychological help in time, and climate policy risks hitting households and businesses hard.
content.extendedDescription:
The social contract is faltering. Sweden now has one of the EU's highest unemployment rates, with young people hit hardest. Meanwhile, many feel that the consequences for high-volume offences such as assault, theft and fraud are too weak. Young people also wait too long for psychological support when they are struggling. Alongside this, concern is growing that climate policy is being designed in ways that harm both household finances and climate effectiveness. Together, this paints a clear picture: today's society is not meeting young people's needs or expectations for the future.

Centerpartiets Ungdomsförbund is therefore launching the report “Samhällskontrakt för unga”, presenting 28 reform proposals on education, mental health, the labour market, safety and the green transition.

content.title: Shared ground rules for preparedness – translating political ambitions into operational capability
content.description: Essential services are expected to continue during crises and war. Yet shared, practical ground rules defining this are lacking. How can political ambitions become operational capability, and what is needed to connect responsibility, requirements and implementation?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's total defence depends on public services and businesses functioning even during crises and war. Yet current work is marked by unclear requirements, uneven application and a lack of shared measures of preparedness capability, with concrete consequences for planning, procurement and implementation.

Clearer structures for responsibility, requirements and methods are needed, along with a better connection between political ambitions and operational reality. Shared frameworks offer one approach, with standardisation among several tools. But these frameworks work only when consistently applied across organisational boundaries.

The seminar discusses translating preparedness ambitions into operational capability. What is needed to clarify requirements and connect responsibility with implementation? The discussion is organised with Krisledningspodden and moderated by Mats Bohman.

content.title: The other side of the medal – insecure living conditions, financial stress and an uncertain future
content.description: Behind medals and high rankings, elite athletes struggle financially. They dedicate their lives to representing Sweden at the highest level, but when their careers end, the future is often uncertain. Sickness benefits and pensions are parts of the social security system that many take for granted, yet they fall short for elite athletes.
content.extendedDescription:
Contrary to what many believe, most people competing for medals for Sweden face finances that do not add up. Half struggle to make ends meet – and more than 200 elite athletes have quit in four years. Two in three Paralympians are considering quitting for financial reasons. Four in ten applicants for SOK's scholarship live below the minimum subsistence level.

What can the social partners do to improve elite athletes' living conditions? What can be resolved through collective agreements, and what requires changes to legislation and regulations? Are there lessons to learn from the cultural sector?

Elite athletes' lives are shaped by training periods, competitions and irregular incomes. They rarely fit into a social insurance system designed to support people in long-term employment. This disadvantages elite athletes, whose careers have peaks and troughs in income and workload. They lack sufficient protection in the event of injury, illness or parental leave. When their careers end, their pensions are often negligible.

content.title: Robust electronic communications — how do we ensure they work in crisis and war?
content.description: Electronic communications are essential to the operation of vital services. In crisis and war, systems come under pressure while dependencies and demands increase. How do we ensure not just availability, but actual functionality, even during major disruptions?
content.extendedDescription:
Electronic communications are a fundamental requirement for society to function in crisis and war. When networks and systems are affected, consequences can be immediate and extensive.

Disruptions quickly hit central functions, and dependencies between systems amplify vulnerabilities, while demands for availability, robustness and cooperation increase in a system with many mutually dependent participants. How do we ensure that electronic communications are not only built to be robust, but actually work when they are truly needed?

The seminar focuses on how electronic communications can be strengthened to sustain essential services, and what requirements are needed to ensure functionality in both the public sector and business. The discussion is held in cooperation with Krisledningspodden, with Mats Bohman as moderator.

content.title: Norrbotten — Sweden's Arctic
content.description: As part of the Arctic territory and a substantial part of the Swedish Arctic, Norrbotten differs from the rest of the country. Not only in its climate, but in many issues taken for granted as national election issues.
content.extendedDescription:
Join a roundtable discussion on the Swedish Arctic!

Important trade routes run straight through the Arctic, and many major powers meet in what has now become a geopolitically and strategically highly significant part of the world. This year, the EU and Sweden are presenting new Arctic strategies.

Norrbotten is a substantial part of the Swedish Arctic and, as in the rest of the territory, local communities form the core of what we call the Arctic, whether the issue is strategic raw materials, preparedness, research or tourism.

Are the issues that will shape this year's election campaign equally relevant to Norrbotten and Arctic Sweden, or do they reflect only challenges in Stockholm? For example, there is virtually no unemployment along the Arctic Circle; the sparse population and long distances create difficulties but also offer advantages.

content.title: 92 per cent goes up in smoke — who takes responsibility for plastic?
content.description: Despite ambitious environmental targets and world-leading waste systems, only 8 per cent of all plastic placed on the Swedish market is currently recycled. Meanwhile, more than 75 per cent is incinerated to produce district heating and electricity.
content.extendedDescription:
Plastic incineration accounts for 7 per cent of Sweden's national emissions and almost all of district heating's climate impact. This is a problem for both the climate and competitiveness. Through emissions trading and a fee to the EU, Sweden pays billions every year for these emissions — costs that risk increasing unless the waste system changes.

At the same time, stakeholders across the plastic value chain want to move in the same direction: energy companies need more recycling to reduce emissions and costs, plastic producers need recycled material to meet climate targets and forthcoming quota requirements, and municipalities and consumers expect real circularity.

But plastic is trapped in a system that was not designed for circulation and where responsibility is fragmented. The seminar brings together industry, politicians and municipalities to discuss how policy instruments and incentives can reduce emissions, lower costs and strengthen competitiveness.

content.title: How do we get construction and essential energy renovations moving?
content.description: The construction sector faces a critical challenge. Despite accounting for around 11% of Sweden's GDP and being central to both growth and societal development, neither construction nor necessary energy renovations have accelerated at the required pace. The EU's new directives set clear requirements.
content.extendedDescription:
The EU's energy-efficiency requirements (EED & EPBD) concern not only climate ambitions but now also stronger preparedness and a more resilient society.
Much activity is currently stalled, while pressure to modernise, transition and renovate is growing rapidly.

The event explores why construction and energy renovations have yet to gain momentum and what obstacles, opportunities and solutions exist amid uncertainty. We discuss the new requirements, why they exist and how they contribute to both the climate transition and resilience in Sweden's building stock.

Discussions between business representatives and leading members of parliament bring different perspectives on stimulating construction and renovation. The focus is on how industry, politics and other stakeholders can jointly create the conditions to get the construction and energy renovations needed for Sweden's future under way.

content.title: Can we afford not to invest in water and wastewater infrastructure?
content.description: A recently revised forecast of municipal investment needs in water and wastewater shows that needs through 2040 still amount to hundreds of billions, while municipalities are falling behind the required investment pace. Charges continue to rise.
content.extendedDescription: Swedish municipal water and wastewater organisations need to invest at least SEK 560 billion by 2040, according to the 2023 investment report. An updated report will be presented in spring 2026. Municipalities are not keeping investment in line with needs, for several reasons. Because investments are financed by borrowing and no accumulated funds are available, financing costs are passed on through customer charges to Sweden's property owners, homeowners, housing cooperatives and tenants. Higher charges may make politicians hesitate, but can we really afford not to invest in water and wastewater? And if customers are not to pay for everything, where should the money come from?
content.subject: Economy
speakerTitles: Water Network and Asset Management Strategist

content.title: Communities are built on water – what do the parties propose ahead of the 2026 election?
content.description: Sweden lacks a coherent water policy, although society and prosperity depend on water access. Climate change challenges both water quality and quantity. Challenges vary greatly between municipalities, and responsibility is shared among around 30 public authorities.
content.extendedDescription:
Water is an essential societal resource, and without functioning water and wastewater systems, society grinds to a halt.

Sweden's water infrastructure – pipes, waterworks and treatment plants – needs substantial investment. Yet significant funding is missing each year to meet demands arising from ageing systems, climate change, preparedness and new EU legislation. Overall, SEK 560 billion must be invested by 2040 to secure future water supplies. Households, business, welfare services, public authorities and civil society must know and trust that society is sufficiently prepared to meet everyone's requirements for robustness, resilience and reliable water and wastewater services. Although water affects everything from defence and industry to rural development and environmental policy, it lacks a clear political home. As a result, one of society's most fundamental functions risks falling through the cracks.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: How can cleaning staff free up healthcare resources?
content.description: Healthcare is struggling with both skills shortages and sickness absence. How can it free up more time for direct patient care by having professional providers handle cleaning and service tasks?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar examines how healthcare's core expertise can be used more effectively by removing tasks that do not require healthcare training. Today, nurses and assistant nurses often perform service tasks such as cleaning, washing dishes, making beds and transporting patients, reducing the time available for direct patient care. By giving professional service providers greater responsibility for these tasks, healthcare staff can spend more time on what they are trained for: medical and nursing care.
We present examples, data and best practice and discuss the potential effects on patient safety, working conditions and access to care. Representatives of the facility management industry and the public sector take part.

content.description: Work-related crime in the cleaning industry harms employees, responsible businesses, municipalities and society. Unscrupulous operators exploit workers and circumvent rules. content.title: Self-regulation of advertising
content.description: Self-regulation is a tool for credible, responsible advertising. As the design and distribution of advertising change, trust in advertising becomes more critical. How can self-regulation remain a relevant, effective and legitimate tool in Sweden and in relation to EU legislation?
content.extendedDescription:
Since Reklamombudsmannen was established in 2009, the advertising we encounter has changed substantially. Today, advertising is everywhere: on social media, in podcasts, in games and in public spaces. The boundaries between information, entertainment and advertising have become increasingly blurred.
Meanwhile, EU legislative work affects Sweden's advertising frameworks and rules. New demands are being placed on the interaction between EU legislation, national laws and self-regulation.
Self-regulation is a central part of society's infrastructure and a tool used in several areas, including credible and responsible advertising. But as the design and distribution of advertising change, trust in advertising becomes more crucial than ever.

content.title: From fossil fuel dependence to e-fuel producer – how do we get there?
content.description: Europe has awakened to a new security situation, but our energy system remains dependent on imported fossil fuels.
content.extendedDescription:
With abundant fossil-free electricity, a strong industrial base and leading innovators, Sweden has a concrete opportunity not only to reduce dependence but to become a leading European e-fuel producer.

Can this development be accelerated?

Hydrogen and e-fuel value chains are taking shape, connecting electricity, industry and transport in new ways. But obstacles remain: an uncertain investment climate, slow permitting processes and a lack of long-term rules hold back a transition Sweden should be leading.

This seminar starts from Sweden's strengths and discusses what is needed to turn potential into reality. What obstacles must be removed? And who needs to act?
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament and Deputy Chair

content.title: From vulnerability to strategic strength – industry's role in Europe's new reality
content.description: How can industry move from vulnerability to strategic strength? How do we ensure that industry becomes a cornerstone of Sweden's and Europe's security and competitiveness? And what political and industrial choices are needed now to strengthen Sweden's long-term ability to act?
content.extendedDescription: An unsettled world has put global value chains and their vulnerabilities in the spotlight. As geopolitical uncertainty increases and the world becomes more regionalised, security of supply, access to raw materials and industrial capacity have become central to both competitiveness and security. Meanwhile, European industry is under pressure from China's aggressive industrial policy and increasingly intense global competition. Over the past year, the steel industry has been at the centre of trade policy shifts, an early indication of steel's role as a strategic resource. What first became evident in the steel sector is now emerging in more and more parts of industry.
content.subject: EU
speakerTitles: Chair of the Municipal Executive Board

content.title: When one in five parents struggles with mental health – who supports the families?
content.description: One in five parents in Sweden experiences mental ill health, but few receive timely support. Almost half want practical help, yet only 10% of municipalities offer it. How can early, coordinated interventions reach families at risk of falling through the cracks?
content.extendedDescription:
One in five parents in Sweden experiences mental ill health, but too few receive timely support. Almost half want practical help such as support at home, respite and assistance with daily routines, yet only 10% of municipalities offer it. Group-based support is also widely lacking despite parents wanting it to share experiences and reduce isolation.

The seminar brings together politicians, authorities, civil society and professionals in social services, psychiatry and parenting support.
MFoF presents the report Stärkt föräldraskapsstöd till föräldrar med psykisk ohälsa eller kognitiva svårigheter; Bräcke diakoni shares experience from TrUSt and Homestart; NSPH highlights the target group's needs.

The round table discusses how coordinated support can reach parents in time, civil society's role when welfare provision falls short, and accessible interventions for the most vulnerable, including parents new to Sweden.

The proposals are summarised in a panel discussion.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: A new election, new opportunities – what is the future of new main railway lines?
content.description: New main railway lines affect Sweden's growth, skills provision and climate transition. The project is paused, but the 2026 election could change that. How do we bring the issue into the election campaign and onto the next government's agenda?
content.extendedDescription:
New main railway lines are crucial to increasing railway capacity, shortening journey times and connecting larger labour market regions across Sweden. For Jönköping, strategically located in the centre of southern Sweden, better connections are essential to strengthen business, facilitate commuting and contribute to national growth.

The seminar brings together representatives from politics, think tanks, business and the rail sector to discuss growth, commuting and the future of railways throughout Sweden. How can the new main lines project be revived ahead of the 2026 election and become one of the next government's priorities? Audience contributions are welcome towards the end of the seminar.

Before departure, we gather for 10–15 minutes for an introductory discussion and to wait for everyone. You must bring your own bicycle. We start at Skeppargatan 24 and follow a loop taking about an hour. Breakfast is provided afterwards, and anyone who wishes can stay for further discussion. content.title: Fuel supplies in an unpredictable world – how Sweden can weather the crisis

content.title: What is needed for transparent, reliable data to become Sweden's next competitive advantage?
content.description: Is data driving the next phase of industrial development? Increasing EU requirements, global trade and AI development are making data and digitalisation strategic advantages. How can political decisions and standards strengthen competitiveness while enabling circularity and innovation in Swedish businesses?
content.extendedDescription:
As EU rules and AI change the conditions for sharing information in value chains, structured data is becoming a strategic business asset. Companies able to share, understand and use data now have a chance to move ahead, but a new study finds that 75% of Nordic companies say they are not ready.

At this seminar, politicians and businesses meet to discuss how Sweden can take a stronger leading position. The discussion starts with EU sustainability requirements, under which companies need to share standardised data such as digital product passports containing information about, for example, climate footprints and packaging materials. It will also address how to ensure that the data made available can be trusted, particularly when AI is used in decision-making.

How should responsibility actually be divided between politicians and businesses? How can companies' investments in data be turned from a requirement into business value? And what is needed to build functioning, interoperable data infrastructure?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: ADHD costs society billions – how do we enable functioning everyday lives, work and quality of life?
content.description: ADHD diagnoses are rising rapidly in Sweden, while many families feel support arrives late. Research and public agencies highlight systemic shortcomings. What drives this development, where do gaps arise, and how can support work earlier and better in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
ADHD diagnoses are rising rapidly in Sweden, particularly among children and young people. Meanwhile, healthcare, schools and families describe a system where support often arrives late and many needs are only identified once problems have become extensive.

The seminar focuses particularly on three areas:
• research and systems perspectives
• schools and early intervention
• women and ADHD

Research from Karolinska Institutet points to a need to shift the focus from diagnosis to functioning and earlier support. Meanwhile, Socialstyrelsen highlights significant shortcomings and variations in care.

The discussion examines why diagnoses are increasing, the gaps between research, schools, healthcare and everyday life, and the consequences of late interventions, from schooling to working life.

The seminar is a moderated panel discussion bringing together perspectives from research, healthcare, schools, working life and users. The focus is on solutions, concrete experiences and changes needed to make everyday life work better in practice.

No preparation is required.

content.title: Precision medicine — a healthcare cost or Sweden's next engine of growth?
content.description: Precision medicine is highlighted as a key to the healthcare of the future, with the potential to improve patient outcomes and strengthen Sweden's competitiveness in life sciences. Despite strong research and advanced care, implementation in Swedish healthcare remains slow.
content.extendedDescription:
Precision medicine can both improve patient outcomes and strengthen Sweden's competitiveness in life sciences. Yet implementation in Swedish healthcare remains slow.

What is needed to make better use of these strengths and improve Sweden's position as a country for clinical trials and precision medicine? What decisions are needed to make precision medicine a strategic engine of growth for Sweden, and how can we attract investment and innovation?

Participants from politics, healthcare and industry come together to discuss how implementation can be accelerated and Sweden's position strengthened. Contributors include representatives from Sahlgrenska Universitetssjukhuset, SwedenBIO and AstraZeneca.

content.title: An industrial platform for sustainability innovation
content.description: How can collaboration between business, innovation and technology help Swedish industry achieve its climate targets?
content.extendedDescription:
BridgeHouse™, a national innovation platform from AstraZeneca, Scania and RISE, will be launched during Almedalsveckan. Its aim is to promote innovation, competitiveness and sustainable technology to help Swedish industry reach its climate targets. The initiative is supported by the government and co-funded by Vinnova.
On the Tech Arena stage, Per Alfredsson, CEO of AstraZeneca AB, Christian Levin, CEO of Scania, and Malin Frenning, CEO of RISE, present the vision behind the initiative. They explain why leading players from different parts of Swedish business are choosing to collaborate across traditional sector boundaries, and what role innovation can play in meeting climate targets for 2030, 2045 and beyond.
The discussion is moderated by Magnus Björsne, CEO of BioVentureHub and Head of BioVenture Innovation Unit, AstraZeneca.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: When no one has the full picture – cooperation for northern Sweden's development
content.description: Northern Sweden is undergoing rapid and extensive change. Major industrial investments, new establishments and growing flows of people, goods and energy affect how our communities develop, simultaneously and in close interaction.
content.extendedDescription:
To better understand what is coming, analysis company Polar Associates has mapped development at system level: which investments are planned, where they are happening, who is driving them and how they connect in time and space. A clear picture emerges: many elements are developing in parallel, and their interdependencies are strengthening.

Against this backdrop, we invite you to a conversation bringing together several perspectives. Together with and more voices, we explore what these developments mean here and now.

This is a conversation in which no one has the whole picture, but together we can get closer to it.

content.title: Military defence moves forward — threats, risks, challenges and solutions
content.description: Försvarsmakten faces extensive rearmament, technological development and demands for greater resilience. At the same time, public support, the right skills and effective NATO integration are needed. What challenges does the Supreme Commander face, and how can he address current and future threats?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's security situation has changed rapidly, placing high demands on Försvarsmakten. Expansion of equipment and personnel must take place alongside a technological shift in weapons systems. Society's resilience also needs to be strengthened more broadly across civilian and military organisations. NATO membership brings new opportunities, but also requirements for interoperability and cooperation. The legitimacy of defence rests on public support and trust, while the right skills and leadership are crucial to success in the current situation.
- How can Försvarsmakten attract and retain the right skills?
- What investment is needed to meet the technological shift?
- How can society's resilience and civil defence be strengthened?
- How can public support and the will to defend be maintained?
- How can effective and rapid NATO integration be ensured?
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Food or the environment – must Sweden choose?
content.description: Sweden faces a choice: how do we produce more food without compromising the environment and climate? As preparedness, costs and climate exert pressure, conflicting goals become clear. Are food and the environment at odds – and who decides what matters most?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish food production is affected by several politically determined societal goals. Ambitious climate and environmental targets must be combined with increased food production, stronger competitiveness and improved food preparedness. Sustainable development must also encompass ecological, social and economic dimensions.
In practice, conflicting goals require trade-offs between interests and perspectives. How can these be managed so they reinforce rather than undermine one another? Do governance, regulations and priorities need reviewing in light of new knowledge, technological development and changing societal needs? How do national choices affect Swedish production, the global environment and food supply? Can ethical approaches provide guidance when societal goals conflict?
This seminar brings together politics, business and research to discuss ways forward for competitive, sustainable and robust Swedish food production.

content.title: Public transport knows how we can achieve the climate targets — how do we get politicians on board?
content.description: Public transport is essential to achieving Sweden's and the EU's climate targets for 2030. Ahead of the 2026 election, we are strengthening our message and highlighting political measures needed to give us a chance of reaching the climate target. Our proposals are ready, but what do politicians say?
content.extendedDescription:
A seminar concluding with a panel debate with politicians.
Svensk Kollektivtrafik, Sveriges Bussföretag and Tågföretagen continue their joint project 4av10. The project aims to improve conditions for public transport and thereby increase its share of motorised journeys. By 2030, four in ten motorised journeys should be by public transport, compared with three in ten today.
We are doing this for road safety, accessibility and the climate on the path towards sustainable communities.

At kollektivtrafiken.se, we present the industry's policy statement with a range of short- and long-term measures. But the climate, growth and fairness also require decisions in parliament and government. Ahead of the 2026 election, we are highlighting three issues that are particularly important for a future built on sustainable travel.

content.title: Kreativa Sverige in practice – culture, innovation and resilience
content.description: Culture and creativity play an increasing role in innovation and societal transition, while Europe accelerates through major initiatives. What paths lie ahead for the cultural and creative industries, taking the societal transition in northern Sweden as a starting point?
content.extendedDescription:
In times of crisis, uncertainty and rapid change, traditional solutions are insufficient. Culture and creativity offer new perspectives, critical thinking and the ability to make complex societal issues understandable and therefore open to change.

The Kreativa Sverige strategy has highlighted cultural and creative industries as a strategic resource for Sweden's development. Meanwhile, a European movement is growing in which culture's role in innovation and societal transition is increasingly evident, particularly through initiatives such as EIT Culture & Creativity and New European Bauhaus.

A central question remains: how can Sweden better harness the potential of cultural and creative industries?

content.title: How innovative may schools be – where should exploration happen if not in schools?
content.description: School practice rests on research, proven experience and clear governing documents. Yet pupils' circumstances, society's needs and forms of knowledge are changing rapidly. This creates tension but also room for action. What responsibility do schools have to develop?
content.extendedDescription:
During Almedalsveckan, Frida Utbildning invites you to a panel on one of schools' most pressing questions: what responsibility and scope for action do schools have to develop in a time of change?

Schools must create good conditions for children's and young people's learning and futures amid rapid societal change. They therefore need both to safeguard proven approaches and explore what is not yet finished, fully understood or regulated.

How much can and should schools themselves explore new methods, tools and forms of learning?
Can we wait for ready-made answers, or must the profession help shape them?

We welcome everyone engaged in school development to pause and think together. We want to share perspectives, listen to different experiences and deepen our collective understanding of schools' responsibilities and scope for action when answers are uncertain but responsibility cannot wait.

content.title: Why are so many children with allergies inadequately treated?
content.description: Pollen allergy is very common among children and young people. It reduces quality of life, lowers school performance and increases the risk of asthma. New data show that more than half of 16-year-olds have uncontrolled disease and only 14% are adequately treated. How can more children get help?
content.extendedDescription:
Is it finally time to address Sweden's most common widespread disease?

One in three people has an allergic disease. A national strategy and national guidelines have now been presented. The strategy emphasises, among other things, that primary care looks after most allergy patients, that access to care varies by socioeconomic status, and that there is a shortage of allergy specialists.

What happens now? Is this the moment when care for what may be Sweden's most common widespread disease takes a step forward, receives resources and becomes a priority?

What do the regions need to do to make primary care governance work, increase fairness and train more allergists? And what is the state doing?

Join an evening of knowledge about allergies, with three themes, from 17-19 in our garden. Hot food and drinks will be available, with opportunities to mingle.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Chair of the Regional Executive Board

content.title: Security for workers – can we really not afford it?
content.description: Sick pay deductions, dental care, pensions and unemployment insurance are identified as priority issues for members in the 2026 election. But can we afford reforms in areas that matter to workers, or not?
content.extendedDescription:
The past few years have been financially tough for many people. Half of Handels' members identify the economy, household finances and social security systems as the most important areas for politicians to decide on after the next election. Specific issues such as abolishing the qualifying deduction from sick pay, cheaper dental care, better pensions and stronger unemployment insurance are identified as priorities for Handels' members.

At the same time, many politicians say society cannot afford it. Is the era of important political reforms for workers really over, or is it more a question of willingness and priorities?

Taking Handels' election issues as a starting point, political representatives from several parties discuss the financial scope for reforms in each area.

content.title: Choosing upper secondary education – too early and too difficult?
content.description: Industry has a substantial need for skills and new recruits. Industrial companies top lists of attractive employers, yet interest in the education leading to them is low. Could a revised upper secondary structure with broader entry routes and gradual choices meet industry's skills needs?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish industry underpins welfare, growth and our ability to remain strong in crises. Yet Industrirådet's skills analysis identifies serious challenges in every industrial sector. These threaten not only defence capability, production, innovation and competitiveness, but also the green transition.

Is today's upper secondary structure, based on early specialisation choices, one reason too few students take industry-relevant courses? Could broader entry routes and gradual choices be part of the solution? The 15-year-olds choosing their education may lack the decision-making skills the current system requires.

Could a new upper secondary structure also improve gender balance, increase the number of students completing school and help them establish themselves in the labour market? Let us discuss how a new path for Swedish upper secondary education could benefit both industry and the future of Sweden's young people.

content.title: How can educational research become relevant and accessible in schools and teacher education?

The seminar addresses scientific quality and relevance, and how the search engine can contribute to greater access to research and increased engagement in educational research.

content.title: Job matching in crisis – unemployment and skills shortages divide Sweden
content.description: Sweden is divided by large differences in unemployment, with high unemployment and skills shortages in some regions and low unemployment elsewhere. How can unemployed people be given the right conditions to take jobs, municipalities secure skills and the state strengthen the labour market nationwide?
content.extendedDescription: Unemployment in Sweden is falling, but regional differences persist. Norrbotten has unemployment of 3.8 per cent, Dalarna 5.2 and Skåne 8.9 per cent, reflecting major differences in education levels, demographics and business structures. Counties with more highly educated residents and diversified labour markets fare better, while regions with larger foreign-born populations and greater dependence on individual industries face bigger challenges. Meanwhile, participation in labour market programmes is declining despite growing needs, risking deeper divides. This comes as many employers struggle to recruit the right skills, creating a growing mismatch in the labour market and reinforcing regional imbalances. What political action is needed for the state to support Sweden's municipalities and businesses and improve their conditions for recruiting skills? And how can unemployed people have better opportunities to enter the labour market?
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: The curse of agreements — when political deals become obstacles to action
content.description: Politics is increasingly bound by agreements between parties, providing stability but potentially reducing the ability to act and respond. How is trust in politics affected when agreements take precedence and risk creating deadlock while the world around us changes?
content.extendedDescription:
The Swedish labour market model rests on trust and collective agreements that evolve with working life and society. Politics, by contrast, is moving towards more agreements between parties, from Decemberöverenskommelsen to Januariavtalet and Tidöavtalet. These can create stability, but also risk locking politics into lists of commitments when rapid adaptation is needed.

When room for manoeuvre is constrained in advance, the dialogue that has long enabled effective interaction between politics and the social partners is reduced. This affects the ability of politics to address issues that directly shape working life.

Where is the boundary between necessary stability and lost freedom to act? Unionen brings together a panel to discuss the benefits and limitations of agreements — and how politics can adapt to a changing world without jeopardising parliamentary stability.

content.title: AI at work: who sets the rules?
content.description: AI is changing working life rapidly, promising more productive processes and a better-matched labour market. Yet concerns include unemployment, discrimination, privacy, stress and reduced employee influence. The question is therefore increasingly important: who sets the rules for AI at work?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is entering more areas of working life, promising new ways of working, more efficient processes and better information for decisions. Yet it is often introduced before structures that give employees influence, transparency and security are in place. This increases the risks associated with AI alongside its promises: greater unemployment, discrimination, threatened privacy and increased stress.

Unionen's data shows how widespread AI use is in business, focusing on recruitment and variations in transparency and influence between workplaces. This raises questions that employers, employees and politicians must address: how can we ensure that the skills development needed for successful AI implementation exists and works?

Unionen presents new survey results from its workplace branches and members, providing insights into how well prepared employees and employers are for the transition. The question is: who sets the rules when technology changes work?

content.title: When life continues – reducing the silence after childhood cancer treatment
content.description: After childhood cancer, the goal is not just survival but quality of life. Childhood cancer care saves lives, but complications such as hearing loss can occur. Today, more than 8 in 10 children diagnosed with cancer in Sweden survive – but who takes responsibility for life afterwards?
content.extendedDescription:
The return to everyday life can be marked by late complications. Medicines are central to several treatments but can also cause permanent hearing loss. For children, this can mean lifelong difficulties at school, in relationships and later at work.

In a seminar involving the audience and making the “silence after treatment” visible, we discuss how a stronger preventive approach can reduce hearing damage: early, systematic follow-up, appropriate support and consideration of quality of life from the treatment-planning stage. Our question is simple and urgent: how do we ensure children who survive cancer also enjoy the best possible quality of life afterwards, while reducing the risk of silence after treatment?

content.title: Forest policy – how smaller family forest owners are affected
content.description: The debate about forests has been heated in recent years. Forestry companies are usually pitted against environmental organisations in a polarising way. But how are Sweden's family forest owners affected by current policy and by the parties' proposals ahead of the election?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has 300 000 forest owners. They are often overlooked in the debate about national forest policy, where active forestry is set against a conservation perspective. As EU legislation is to be implemented in Sweden and a comprehensive forestry inquiry presents a range of national proposals, questions about economic conditions, usage rights, compensation and public-agency responsibilities become highly significant for individual forest owners. Many parties say they care about forest owners' profitability. But how do their different proposals affect family forest owners – and their finances?
Landshypotek Bank and Föreningen Skogen have asked the parliamentary parties about their forest policies and invited all of them to this seminar. The starting point is a discussion from the family forest owner's perspective.
The discussion aims to clarify what is needed from policy to provide long-term sustainability, willingness to invest and economic empowerment for the country's 300 000 family forest owners.

content.title: How do we make culture and participation a natural part of children and young people's everyday lives?
content.description: Children and young people are often described as the future, but we live here now, and the best way to face the future is together – children, young people and adults in dialogue.
content.extendedDescription: Are you curious about working with young people's influence and participation? Come and listen to, talk to and ask questions of us (KC+), young people from KulturCrew Skåne. Here you will find ideas and examples that benefit young people in practice. KulturCrew started in Skåne in 2016 and now operates in 13 counties in Sweden. The method comes from Denmark, and the aim is for children and young people's voices to be heard and taken seriously. In KulturCrew, we work together as a group and learn how to turn an idea into reality. We cooperate with the professional cultural sector across all art forms. Some questions we want to raise: how can every child's right to culture be fulfilled? Why not invest in what young people want? What is the difference between influence and participation? How do you build an association with young people in leadership roles? What are the benefits of working with youth participation and young event organisers, with a focus on culture? Who is responsible for increasing young people's participation? It is time to move beyond the planning stage and show that young people's voices count!

content.title: Parent of a transgender person: the struggle to keep your child alive
content.description: What is everyday life like for the parent of a transgender person? The struggle to get schools and authorities to follow the law and the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The struggle to make daily life work. The struggle to keep your child alive.

When the child Jenny knew as her daughter was eleven, he showed her his diary.
‘My name is Love and I am eleven. I am a boy, but my family thinks I am a girl. They don't understand anything.’
The talk Transmamman – min berättelse is about Jenny's struggle as the parent of a transgender child.

Jenny has advocated for LGBTQI+ rights for many years. She moved to Gotland with her family after working for a year as Operations Manager at RFSL Sjuhärad. content.title: Hope that saves lives – creating paths forward despite mental ill health
content.description: More and more people live with mental ill health, excluded from work and education. But there are approaches that break isolation and support recovery through community, structure and long-term commitment. How can political decisions and new pathways increase participation, improve quality of life and reduce costs to society?
content.extendedDescription:
How can community, structure and long-term support create paths forward when mental ill health limits opportunities to study and work?
Do people with mental ill health receive the right support in your municipality, or are there gaps along the path to work and education?

The discussion opens with a member's personal story, followed by an introduction to the Clubhouse model, an established approach to work-oriented rehabilitation found in more than 370 locations worldwide, including 20 in Sweden.

Drawing on experience and evaluations, we discuss how the model can support recovery, strengthen pathways to education and financial independence, and reduce the need for healthcare interventions. Rickard Bracken, Secretary General of Mind, shares perspectives on growing loneliness and the need for meaningful social connections, based on a recent survey.

What is needed to give more people access to effective rehabilitation, and how can proven models be scaled up?
With us, no one falls through the cracks. We show how it works.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Nanoplastics and human health
content.description: Nanoplastics are present in air, water, food and the human body. Research shows that these particles can cross biological barriers and affect the body's organs and systems. What does current research say about health risks, societal impacts and the need for cooperation?
content.extendedDescription:
Nanoplastics consist of extremely small plastic particles that can cross the body's biological barriers, such as the intestinal barrier, the blood–brain barrier and the placenta. Studies show that microplastics and nanoplastics can be found in several organs and tissues, where they can contribute to inflammation, oxidative stress and effects on cell function. Research points to possible links with effects on the nervous system, cardiovascular system, hormonal balance and reproductive health.

During the seminar, Allatra Sweden presents an interdisciplinary view of nanoplastics from a public health perspective. The event takes the form of a seminar with a presentation. No prior knowledge is required.

The aim is to increase knowledge of nanoplastics as a growing societal challenge and create a constructive discussion about the need for further research, preventive measures and international cooperation between researchers, decision-makers and civil society.

content.title: Why is a national resource centre for internationally adopted people needed?
content.description: Today, adoptees themselves often help other adoptees with questions about origins, identity and contact with authorities. This shows that society's support is insufficient. Responsibility must shift from individuals to a safe, professional and lasting structure. What do adopted people say?
content.extendedDescription:
The event takes the form of a discussion focused on the question: why is a national resource centre for internationally adopted people needed? Today, adoptees themselves often help other adoptees with questions about origins, identity, documents, rights and contact with authorities. This shows that society's support is insufficient and that responsibility must shift from individuals to a safe, professional and lasting structure.

During the discussion, we highlight the voices of internationally adopted people and examine the need for coordinated support, legal guidance and knowledge among the relevant authorities. Lawyer Lisa Gauffin Dahlin and a representative of the Chilean Consulate have been invited to contribute legal perspectives and information about how the consulate can be an important link in these matters. Participants do not need to prepare in advance.

content.title: Molecules as resilience – what role do the chemical and process industries play in preparedness?
content.description: More than ninety per cent of the products we use every day depend on the chemical and process industries. These industries currently rely heavily on imported raw materials from fossil sources. This makes Sweden and Europe vulnerable to geopolitical crises and disruptions in global supply chains.
content.extendedDescription:
Transformed chemical and process industries using a greater share of domestic bio-based and circular raw materials could become a cornerstone of secure supplies and stronger defence capabilities in Sweden and Europe. The benefits are clear, but how do we achieve domestic supply chains independent of fossil resources while maintaining competitiveness? In this seminar, we outline the path towards resilient, strong and green chemical and process industries and the obstacles that industry, politics and the market must overcome together.

Together with industry representatives, defence experts and politicians, we explore the role the Swedish chemical and process industries play, and could play, in Sweden's preparedness for crisis or conflict. What needs to be done, and who needs to act, to create more robust chemical and process industries that can support Sweden's and Europe's defence capabilities?

Breakfast is served from 8:30

Moderator: Hanna Paradis, Klimatledande Processindustri

content.title: Two universities and philanthropists collaborating on societal challenges
content.description: How can universities collaborate with each other and philanthropists to respond faster to societal challenges despite their long-term structures, strengthening their contribution to society?
content.extendedDescription: Universities have four tasks: research, teaching, innovation and service to society. When new challenges emerge, universities, built around long-term work, sometimes struggle to act quickly enough to offer the best possible support. Collaboration between universities can help by creating greater critical mass and a broader range of specialist knowledge and capabilities. If philanthropists can also be engaged, the potential contribution to society can be substantial. We discuss these issues and give two examples of Göteborgs universitet and Chalmers working with two philanthropists to address a health issue and an urgent educational initiative in refugee camps.

content.title: When roads and railways become congested, is inland shipping the answer?
content.description: Is it time for a new approach and a boost for Swedish inland shipping? What is actually holding back development, and which reforms are needed to move more freight from road and rail to water?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's roads and railways are heavily loaded, and the government is now making historically large investments in maintaining existing infrastructure. Meanwhile, something is rarely discussed in transport policy: spare capacity on our lakes Vänern and Mälaren. Sweden's inland ports could handle a substantially larger share of freight. Moving freight from land to water has long been a political ambition, but without incentives little happens in practice. If we want to reduce congestion, strengthen preparedness and meet climate targets, we cannot keep doing the same things and expect different results.

This seminar presents four proposals for more competitive inland shipping, and a panel of parliamentarians will address how they could be implemented.

content.title: From words to action for more clinical trials in Sweden
content.description: In July 2025, the government commissioned the establishment of a national partnership to strengthen Sweden's role in clinical trials and life sciences. Now it is high time for the partners to unite around that mission. What is needed to make Sweden an attractive location for more clinical trials?
content.extendedDescription:
For Swetrial to become the unifying force that genuinely increases the number of clinical trials, room must be made for trials in everyday healthcare work. Real impact requires regions to take responsibility and, crucially, politicians to issue clear directives with measurable targets. Healthcare often has clear governance, controls and follow-up for production and capacity planning across its services.

With very few exceptions, this is absent for clinical trials, meaning that regions effectively deprioritise them. In other words, how do we move from words to reality?

content.title: Goals, uncertainty and responsibility in managing Baltic Sea fish – where have all the fish gone?
content.description: Management of our fish stocks has failed. Baltic cod has collapsed, and herring stocks are under pressure. Do we need new goals, greater caution and a broader perspective? What responsibility do policymakers, researchers and industry bear for restoring stocks?
content.extendedDescription:
The EU's Common Fisheries Policy starts from a seemingly simple idea: we should be able to catch as much fish as possible without jeopardising stocks' long-term viability. Management involves an extensive process intended to ensure sustainable fishing, with decisions based on scientific advice.

Despite this, several stocks clearly struggle to recover from historical overfishing. Baltic cod stocks have collapsed, and the situation for the Baltic Sea's most important fish species, herring, is worrying.

Our seminar examines today's management system, its shortcomings and how it may affect the developments we see in the Baltic Sea. We highlight proposals to restore fish stocks, including an ecosystem-based, holistic approach to stock management, updated goals and reduced risk-taking in fisheries management. The system needs to change: what responsibility and contribution can and should each stakeholder take?

content.title: What is needed to secure access to vegetables, fruit and berries nationwide in times of crisis?
content.description: What is needed to secure access to vegetables, fruit and berries throughout the country if a crisis comes? Who has responsibility, and who takes it?
content.extendedDescription:
What is on our plates during a crisis or when borders close? Grain storage is currently highlighted as a central element, but a prolonged crisis or serious disruption also requires access to vegetables, fruit and berries. Here, the share of Swedish produce has been declining steadily for a long time. How can access be secured in a crisis? What are the greatest threats? Who is responsible for ensuring these foods are available at all?

In this seminar, we discuss threats to and opportunities for securing access to vegetables, fruit and berries during different crises in Sweden. What does availability look like in different parts of the country? What are the greatest threats relating to cultivation, inputs such as seeds, crop protection, nutrients and water, as well as storage and distribution? What can be done to secure basic availability? What responsibilities lie with central government, municipalities and businesses? And with you?

content.title: The battle over public art
content.description: The so-called one per cent rule means that a fixed share, usually one per cent, of a building investment is allocated to public art. In recent years, the rule and public art have become increasingly politicised, bringing the role of art in society into sharp focus.
content.extendedDescription:
In recent years, public art and the so-called one per cent rule – which allocates a fixed share, usually one per cent, of a building investment to public art – have become politicised, bringing the role of art in society into sharp focus.
The one per cent rule is currently applied by half of the country's municipalities and regions. For several years, however, proposals to abolish or change it have been put forward in many municipalities and regions. Abolishing the rule is also proposed in the much-debated policy document Tidö 2.0. Elsewhere, politicians advocate referendums on public art.
At the same time, opinion polls tell us that many people consider public art important in their local surroundings and feel that it creates safety and a pleasant environment. Because it is accessible to everyone, it is also important for achieving the national cultural policy objectives. For this discussion, we invite politicians who support and oppose the rule.

content.title: Stories from Ukrainian veterans
content.description: What can those who risk their lives to protect Europe tell us about the strength and fragility of life? Ukrainian veterans fight for their families and the future of Europe – how can they reconcile their experiences through the written word, and what can we learn from them?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar we meet Ukrainan veterans from the YMCA Lviv programme and hear their stories. Many are civilians who left their jobs and way of life to defend their families and country. Among them are many artists, teachers, and activists who, having participated in the war for freedom, have unique experiences and insights about life and death.
When veterans have the chance to express themselves, their experience can become a shared asset rather than a personal trauma. What opportunities does art-rehabilitation through literature offer for veterans? How does cooperation with veterans from Scandinavian countries shape the identity of the Defenders of Europe, and what opportunities does a European veterans’ network provide?

content.title: What view of humanity does a society that imprisons 13-year-olds hold?
content.description: What does it say about our view of humanity when children as young as 13 face prison? It exposes a conflict between punishment and care, responsibility and protection. What kind of society do we want to be – one that punishes children or one that invests in their future?
content.extendedDescription:
More and more voices advocate tougher measures against young offenders, including lowering the age of criminal responsibility. But what are the consequences for the individual, the rule of law and society as a whole? Clearly, strong interventions and measures are needed, but prison is hardly the best option.

Through discussions between researchers, professionals, civil society and decision-makers, we examine child development, risk and protective factors, and alternative interventions that can break patterns of crime without making exclusion permanent. Is punishment a solution, or does it risk making the problems worse? We also discuss international experiences and what the Convention on the Rights of the Child means in practice.

content.title: E-methanol: a piece of the puzzle in shipping's transition?
content.description: Shipping is central to the energy transition and the path to net-zero emissions by 2050. Electrification, efficiency and new fuels are needed. What role can e-methanol play? What are its potential and prerequisites in shipping's transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Shipping faces a crucial transition to meet the EU's net-zero emissions target by 2050. Reducing fossil fuel dependence requires a combination of electrification, energy efficiency, changed logistics and new fossil-free fuels. One of the most promising alternatives is e-methanol, an electrofuel made from fossil-free electricity, water and biogenic carbon dioxide.

E-methanol could reduce shipping's climate impact while strengthening Europe's energy security and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels. Building domestic hydrogen and e-fuel production could create new export opportunities for Sweden, strengthen industrial competitiveness and contribute to a more robust energy system.

The seminar discusses e-methanol's role in shipping's transition, the market conditions needed to scale up production and use, and barriers and policy instruments affecting development in Sweden and the EU.

content.title: It is all on the plate – political solutions for health, climate, justice and preparedness
content.description: Sweden's food system drives emissions, ill health and inequality; farmers face pressure and many people cannot afford good food. Yet food systems can strengthen preparedness, public health and the environment – solutions exist. Political courage and decisions grounded in research and farmers' reality are now needed.
content.extendedDescription:
Today's food system harms the climate, health, biodiversity and preparedness, while not everyone has enough to eat. But it could be the opposite. Knowledge and solutions exist. Sustainable food systems can store carbon, strengthen public health and preparedness, feed people and build community. Achieving this requires political decisions and broad public support.

Format:

- Brief introduction to the current food system.
- Presentation of three concrete policy proposals.
- Presentation of guides: practical tools for transition in everyday and working life.
- Panel discussion with civil society and producer and/or research representatives.
- Open questions, inviting active participation from the audience and decision-makers.

We create a solution-oriented discussion bringing different perspectives together and giving politicians the opportunity to respond to the proposals. The focus is on how we can jointly transform the food system, moving from problems to achievable change.
content.subject: Food

content.description: Sweden needs more homes. How can we meet growing housing needs in new ways? Which markets have succeeded in creating new, sustainable and attractive homes even in tougher times? What can we do better in Sweden?
