content.title: The home becomes a war zone – the stark, merciless reality of domestic violence
content.description: Domestic violence is one of our most hidden and critical societal issues: violence that often begins in the name of love but gradually wears people down, isolates them and, in the worst cases, threatens their lives.
content.extendedDescription: This event examines one of our most urgent societal issues: domestic violence. We explore how violence develops, becomes normalised and takes hold behind closed doors, from the first subtle signs to full-scale terror that can shatter both body and mind. We also highlight courage, resistance and the paths out of the darkness in which many still live. The programme combines a lecture, an impassioned address and discussion. Participants will hear realistic accounts of how fear grows, boundaries are erased and the perpetrator's control gradually takes over daily life. At the same time, we highlight the forces that can turn things around: insight, support, knowledge and the courage to say no to violence.

content.title: Choral singing as a political force
content.description: For 150 years, choral singing has played a crucial role in democratic development: in popular movements, the Baltic independence struggle, apartheid's fall in South Africa and now opposition to ICE. How can choral singing play a significant role in Swedish politics and social development today? How can singing strengthen democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
In a seminar featuring singing, we discuss choral singing, which has historically contributed to democratic development but has also been used successfully by dark forces in totalitarian states.

Today, more than half a million Swedes sing in choirs. What makes so many devote time and energy to singing together? What can settings where people listen to one another and cooperate towards a common goal mean in our polarised times?

Choral singing is now mostly discussed in terms of individual health: choir members simply feel good. How can this wellbeing spread to wider settings, to society as a whole and across policy areas? And when choral singing is prescribed, what happens to the singing itself?

content.title: Unequal health: who receives help and who is left out?
content.description: Sweden is more multicultural than ever, yet health inequalities persist. When people do not feel understood, many turn away from support, resulting in poorer health and reduced trust. Cultural awareness is systematically absent from professional practice and education. What must change?
content.extendedDescription:
A moderated panel followed by open audience dialogue. It begins with a brief introduction to how inadequate intercultural awareness in people-facing professions affects health, wellbeing and trust, with concrete examples of costs to individuals and society.

The panel addresses mental health, inclusion and preventive public health work, then examines what is actually needed: from education policy and political decisions to inclusive professional interactions and practical working methods. The conversation moves between lived and practical experience and structural solutions, perspectives rarely brought together. Participants leave with concrete insights and proposals that can influence organisations and system-level decisions.

content.title: Heavy transport in transition – electrification, hydrogen and Europe's competitiveness
content.description: Transport needs to transition while Europe strengthens competitiveness and resilience. How can industry and decision-makers create the right conditions amid rapid technological development and geopolitical uncertainty?
content.extendedDescription:
The transport sector must transition while European industry strengthens competitiveness amid rapid technological development and geopolitical uncertainty. Electrification is the main route for heavy transport, with hydrogen an important complement, particularly for long-distance journeys.

The issue is primarily about creating conditions for innovation, investment and large-scale deployment at the right pace, rather than choosing technologies. Infrastructure, energy systems and regulations must develop alongside industrial investment.
This discussion brings together leading industry representatives to share insights into technological shifts, investment conditions and the policies needed to build a competitive, fossil-free transport system.

content.title: From research and education to defence capability in the Arctic
content.description: In a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty, the connection between research, defence procurement and defence capability has become increasingly clear. The ability to develop, test and introduce new solutions quickly without losing sight of sustainability is crucial, particularly in an Arctic context.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar focuses on how cooperation between academia, industry and total defence can strengthen both Sweden's defence capability and its climate transition, with a particular focus on the Arctic. This is a region with unique conditions that place demands on robustness, logistics and cooperation.

The discussion addresses Arctic test and demonstration environments, skills provision within total defence, innovation, societal resilience and security of supply, among other topics. It explores how security and sustainability interests can go hand in hand when research meets civilian and military needs in strategically critical areas.

Through examples and perspectives from different stakeholders, Luleå tekniska universitet illustrates how closer interaction between academia, industry, society and defence can contribute to both national security and long-term innovation and competitiveness.

content.title: Can collaboration and technology solve the teacher shortage?
content.description: Securing teacher supply while maintaining quality, equity and accessibility matters for schools and is crucial to Sweden's competitiveness. Today's system cannot meet needs nationwide. New ways of working that use modern technology are therefore needed.
content.extendedDescription:
Through close collaboration with municipalities and other universities, Luleå tekniska universitet has developed models making teacher education accessible throughout northern Sweden and, in practice, nationwide. University collaboration has also strengthened provision in smaller subjects and built strong research environments.

Meanwhile, new technologies can ease teachers' workloads, support pupils' learning and provide more tailored, interactive teaching support. How can we combine next-generation technologies with new approaches to teacher supply without losing sight of teachers' vital role and the importance of classrooms?

Effective teacher education is crucial for effective schools here and now, but the consequences reach much further. This is where we secure Sweden's future competitiveness and ability to address societal challenges, particularly in STEM.

content.title: Education based on scientific evidence — what does it mean?
content.description: It goes without saying that education should be based on research. At the same time, this raises questions about which research is relevant, how it is made accessible and how it can be used in the school system.
content.extendedDescription:
The purpose of education is complex and requires insights from several fields of research. There are no simple answers or single research approach that can meet every need. Instead, we need a broad and nuanced understanding of what knowledge is relevant to the school system. Education professionals also need a central role in determining what knowledge is needed in practice. This raises questions about research literacy and requires educational research to be made accessible and useful in practice.

The seminar is organised by ULF (Utbildning, Lärande, Forskning), a collaboration between Swedish higher education institutions offering teacher education and school authorities on practice-oriented educational research. During the seminar, people with different roles and connections to the school system come together to discuss what education based on scientific evidence means.

content.title: The lack of rehabilitation – a loss for individuals and society
content.description: People with neurological or rheumatic diseases unnecessarily lose their ability to work. Medicines can help, but rehabilitation is often the only treatment enabling people to function in everyday life. Unfortunately, many receive no rehabilitation at all – a major loss for individuals and society.
content.extendedDescription:
We invite you to a discussion-based seminar focusing on patients' perspectives. We highlight what rehabilitation can mean for individuals' ability to live independently and for society through lower costs for benefits, personal assistance and other support.
Several reports show that access to rehabilitation is low, has declined and is unequal. The Health and Medical Services Act is clear: everyone is entitled to rehabilitation. Responsibility is shared by regions and municipalities, contributing to shortcomings and inequality.

Sweden faces skills shortages across much of the labour market. With appropriate support and rehabilitation, many people could remain employed and contribute to society and their own livelihoods.

Investment in rehabilitation pays off in several ways. Society gains higher tax revenues and lower costs for sickness compensation and personal assistance, healthcare needs decrease, and individuals' autonomy and independence increase.

content.title: Is there a connection between social media and loneliness?
content.description: In 2023, the World Health Organization (WHO) classified loneliness as an urgent global health threat. Although social media creates new opportunities for connection and community, there are indications that being on social platforms does not always contribute to them.
content.extendedDescription:
There is increasing discussion of social media's impact on people's health and wellbeing. At the same time, involuntary loneliness is spreading through society. A new Nordic report from If shows that half of all Swedes experience involuntary loneliness to varying degrees.

The report offers deeper insights into loneliness among Swedes and other Nordic populations, including its relationship with social media use. It also highlights what parents worry about most regarding their children's future. Social media's impact on health stands out clearly.

In Almedalen, If brings together participants from business, politics, academia and civil society to discuss how loneliness and social media are connected, how to work preventively and what good examples exist of social media actually reducing loneliness.

content.title: How can policy strengthen schools' work against violence towards children?
content.description: Children living with violence are in every classroom, but far too few are identified. Schools have a clear mandate but often lack the conditions to act. What political measures are needed to change this?
content.extendedDescription:
At least 210 000 children in Sweden are estimated to live with domestic violence – around one in ten. The consequences are serious: increased risk of mental ill health, difficulties at school and poorer life chances.

Yet few of these children access society's support services. Only a small proportion tell school staff, and schools account for a very limited share of child welfare reports, despite being where children spend most time outside the home.

Teachers' and school leaders' experiences point not to a lack of willingness but to inadequate conditions: uncertainty about signs of violence, fear of making mistakes and insufficient support in difficult situations.

The panel discussion starts from these problems, bringing together parliamentary parties' education policy representatives to discuss political measures that could strengthen schools' ability to identify and act on suspicions that a child lives with violence at home.

content.title: If water runs out, preparedness stops
content.description:
Water is more than a natural resource: it is fundamental to the resilience of our entire society and essential for Swedish food production to function.
How can we secure access to clean water most quickly, and what collaboration is needed to strengthen preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
Looking at Sweden's preparedness work, we see that water and food supplies are closely linked. Livsmedelsverket describes food supply and drinking water as one of the country's most central preparedness sectors: everyone must have sufficient safe food and drinking water during crises and, ultimately, war.

For the food industry, water is a critical input, but also essential for hygiene, cleaning, cooling and robust production flows. Preparedness is therefore not just about coping with interruptions but maintaining as much normality as possible. When water supplies work, everyday life works better too: meals are served, businesses keep operating and people's security improves. This requires close collaboration between businesses, municipalities, authorities and water and wastewater operators.

Preparedness is not created in silos; it is built together. What kind of collaboration is needed, what infrastructure is already in place, and how should it be financed?

content.title: What do Swedes think about climate and biodiversity policy?
content.description: Political decisions are needed to meet climate and biodiversity targets, yet environmental policy is being weakened today in the belief that the public does not support more ambitious measures. But what does research say about Swedes' views on environmental policy measures? What conclusions do politicians draw from the findings?
content.extendedDescription:
Research shows that more policy measures are needed to meet environmental targets for climate and biodiversity. Yet parts of environmental policy have recently been weakened on the grounds that public support is lacking. But what do we actually know about Swedes' attitudes to more concrete environmental policy proposals? The answer matters because attitudes have a major bearing on political feasibility.

The seminar draws on the findings of a new scientific report, 'Svenska folkets attityder till styrmedel för klimat och biologisk mångfald' (Swedish public attitudes to policy instruments for climate and biodiversity). The report is based on a survey in which around 2000 Swedes expressed their views on 30 specific policy measures relating to climate and biodiversity. The survey also examined Swedes' concerns and priorities in environmental policy, and whether attitudes differ between social groups.

The report will be presented at the seminar, followed by a panel discussion with representatives of parliamentary parties.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.

content.title: From guidelines to reality – how do we ensure that menopause care improves?
content.description: Socialstyrelsen has produced new national guidelines for treating menopausal symptoms. This is an important and welcome step. But guidelines alone do not change healthcare: political will, clear responsibilities and follow-up are needed.
content.extendedDescription:
Today, women receive different care depending on where in the country they live. Knowledge levels vary, structures are lacking, and many patients feel they are not properly assessed or offered evidence-based treatment. The new guidelines clarify what should be done – but how do we ensure that it actually happens? What is required of regional political leaders? How can primary care be given the right conditions?
How are the guidelines followed up, and who is accountable if they are not implemented?
Welcome to a discussion about the next step towards equitable, evidence-based menopause care for women throughout the country.

content.title: Young managers are missing, but the future cannot wait. How do we pave the way for the next generation of leaders?
content.description: Young leaders are needed more than ever. But what prevents them from becoming managers? What can established managers contribute, and what is needed from young people today? We need decisive action to create sustainable leadership at a time when the future feels more uncertain than ever.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden and the world are experiencing growing polarisation, economic uncertainty, declining trust in institutions and a labour market changing faster than organisations can adapt. Meanwhile, we face an acute shortage of young managers. Sweden currently has a smaller proportion of young managers than the European average. This is not just a skills problem, but a societal problem.

We bring together young managers and leaders, representatives of business and other sectors to discuss what being a young manager is really like and what happens to an organisation when young people take leadership roles. What are the challenges and success factors? How can organisations be built that young people want to lead and have the opportunity to lead? What does this require of young people themselves and of organisations seeking to secure their skills supply and invest in young managers?

content.title: What role do hunting and hunters play in society?
content.description: Everyone knows hunting is a central part of Sweden's nature conservation, food supply and rural life. Hunters contribute to wildlife management, ecological balance and community. But what other aspects are there to the importance of hunting and hunters in society, today and in the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Hunting is one of Sweden's largest popular movements and a crucial part of its food supply, nature conservation and preparedness. ‘Gilla jakt’ is a podcast on the theme ‘We are hunters — conversations about our role in society’. It will explore life as a hunter, hunting and hunters' role in society, and will be recorded at our outdoor site at 14:00 on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday for release at 17:00.

Jägarnas Riksförbund, which produces the podcast, works to make hunting accessible, sustainable over the long term and knowledge-based. At the same time, we see how regulations, land issues and a widening gap between urban and rural areas risk making things harder for both current and future hunters. A key question is how more people, particularly young people and those without land, can participate in hunting. JRF pursues these issues with the aim of ensuring that hunting remains a natural part of a sustainable Sweden.
content.subject: Animals/nature

content.title: Set research free — it is an election year!
content.description: In recent years, the issue of academic freedom has moved beyond higher education into the public sphere. Everyone seems to agree that academic freedom needs defending — the government is even investigating how to strengthen it. But do we agree on what academic freedom means?
content.extendedDescription:
Ever since the first self-governing universities were established in the Middle Ages, teachers and students have defended the right to seek knowledge freely, without political control. In today's debate, the issue ranges from academics' freedom of expression to the very essence of research and higher education, and to a fundamental democratic principle that concerns us all.
Why must academic freedom be protected right now? And can it be combined with growing demands for publicly funded research and higher education to be relevant to society?
This discussion addresses the tension between academic freedom and demands for education and research to benefit society. The panel includes representatives from academia, politics and the media.

content.title: Popular education 2.0: how do we make AI skills Sweden's new basic competency?
content.description: Sweden has an enormous AI skills gap — most white-collar workers see a need for AI, but only a fraction are offered training. How do we move from a few AI professionals to practical education for everyone?
content.extendedDescription:
For Sweden to be competitive, a handful of experts is not enough; we need broad understanding across the population. Realising AI's potential requires a public education effort on the scale of the introduction of universal schooling or the rollout of broadband.

But today's gap is wide. A large majority of working people see an immediate need for AI skills, but only a fraction are offered training and few employers have a plan to meet this need, creating a major skills gap. In this session, we discuss lessons from and challenges in large-scale continuing education in AI. How do we reach all the way into municipal offices and out to small-business owners? We explore how, together, we can build the national AI literacy that the labour market of the future requires.

content.title: Innovation as defence capability: AI-enhanced processes to meet the unexpected
content.description: Försvarsmakten's need to respond to new threats requires Sweden to develop AI-enhanced innovation processes. Adapting our innovation capability to these demands strengthens the entire country's resilience. How can Sweden move from peacetime logic to smarter preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is a world leader in innovation, but our processes are designed for peacetime. In a changing world, working harder is not enough: we must work smarter. We need AI-enhanced innovation processes in which AI is not merely part of the technology but drives the methods, functions and decision-making themselves.

The lessons from Ukraine are clear: rapidly adapting new technology is crucial. This requires a national transition making innovation integral to defence capability. By meeting the military domain's extreme demands for speed and precision, we create methods that strengthen Sweden's innovation capacity as a whole. Advances made to counter sudden threats thus become a catalyst for Swedish competitiveness and public benefit in peacetime too.

How can we build AI solutions that help us innovate more intelligently? How can solutions developed for defence strengthen Sweden as an innovation nation?

content.title: How can public procurement drive reuse in the construction sector?
content.description: Extensive renovation needs risk increasing the construction sector's climate impact. At the same time, there are demands for lower emissions and circular material flows. How can reuse be scaled up, and what role can public procurement play in enabling this development?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces extensive renovation of apartment buildings from the 1960s, 70s and 80s. These investments involve large material flows that, using traditional approaches, risk causing substantial climate impact. Meanwhile, the construction sector and municipal housing companies have ambitious goals for lower emissions, greater resource efficiency and more circular material flows.

Reusing construction products is highlighted as an important part of the solution, as it can reduce the need for newly manufactured materials and thus climate impact. But making reuse an integral part of construction and renovation processes requires changes to working methods, business models and regulations.

Drawing on experience from research, innovation and practical projects, the discussion explores the opportunities and obstacles to scaling up reuse in construction and renovation projects. Where are we today, and what is needed to take the next step? And what does it take for public procurement to serve as a tool in this development?

speakerTitles: Head of Projects and Property Development

content.title: Time to leave the 1980s behind and accelerate electrification
content.description: How do we get electrification moving? Despite high ambitions, electricity use remains at 1980s levels. What measures are needed to accelerate progress? This is crucial to meeting climate targets, securing competitiveness and reducing our need for fossil fuels.
content.extendedDescription: Electrification is too slow. Despite high ambitions, electricity use remains at 1980s levels. Electrification is crucial if we are to meet our climate targets, reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and secure Sweden's competitiveness. Measures are now needed to make the transition easier for both industry and households. These include taxes, industrial policy, permitting processes and a well-functioning energy system. Today, as in the 1980s, we use around 140 TWh of electricity a year, while still using 140 TWh of fossil fuels. We will describe our dialogues with politicians, public authorities and businesses, as well as the sensible proposals we have collected. We will thank the 1980s for their time, because now it is time for the electricity use of the future!

content.title: Why aren't Meta's scam advertisements being stopped?
content.description: Criminal advertising on Facebook and Instagram exploits Swedish media companies and journalists. Every day, Meta distributes around 15 billion scam advertisements and earns more than SEK 4,000 per second from the fraud. Why do the advertisements keep appearing? What is the Swedish media industry doing?
content.extendedDescription:
These scam advertisements cause financial and psychological suffering for innocent people, while Meta earns large sums by publishing the fraud. The advertisements also undermine the credibility of the media outlets being exploited, making them a democratic problem too.

Publishers' organisation Utgivarna and online marketing organisation IAB Sverige have filed DSA complaints and police reports against Meta and its CEO Mark Zuckerberg for offences including fraud and aiding and abetting fraud. A lawsuit in a Swedish court is also being prepared, and Meta has been expelled from IAB Sverige.

Publishers around the world are now cooperating to force Meta to take responsibility, and Swedish media companies have begun discussions with media intermediaries and advertisers about joint action.
content.subject: Media/journalism

content.title: Essential self-care – how university hospitals are leading the transition from hospital to home
content.description: As advanced care moves into the home, person-centred systems are needed to ensure high-quality care. University hospitals need legally sound models for self-care. How can chief nursing officers, heads of administration, patients and relatives together lead a safe transition from hospital to home?
content.extendedDescription: The transformation of healthcare means that increasingly highly specialised care is moving from university hospitals to patients' homes. Maintaining high-quality care and patient safety requires a shift to genuinely person-centred systems, drawing on patients' own resources through safe and well-founded self-care. But as the boundaries between inpatient care, Hospital at Home and patients' own responsibility shift, complex challenges arise. How do we create legally sound models in which information requirements, consent and the allocation of responsibility are based on each individual's unique circumstances and needs? The seminar places CNO/CMO leadership at the heart of this quality-driven transition. We explore how chief nursing officers and heads of administration at management level must lead the development of future self-care together with patients and relatives. We discuss how to move from parallel care structures to coherent, person-centred processes that strengthen patient empowerment and build quality all the way home.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Taxis as a pillar of society — from everyday life to crisis
content.description: How do we secure taxis as a pillar of society and a preparedness resource across the country — and what political decisions are needed locally, regionally and nationally?
content.extendedDescription:
When society needs passenger transport most — during disruptions, extreme weather, pandemics or heightened alert — the capacity must be there. But emergency preparedness is not built in a vacuum. It relies on genuine taxi services and other lawful operators being available in everyday life to provide safe, traceable, high-quality passenger transport throughout Sweden. At the same time, legitimate businesses are under pressure from unlicensed taxis, illegal taxi operations and labour-related crime, undermining both competition and society's actual transport capacity. The seminar brings together experts and decision-makers to discuss how policy, procurement and requirements can strengthen legality, safety and delivery capability — from everyday life to crisis.

When Russia invaded Ukraine, it quickly became clear that the country's resilience was not based solely on military strength. It also relied on civil society's exceptional ability to act when the state could no longer meet every need.

In Ukraine, the scouting movement has organised the collection and distribution of food, clothing and medicines, served as local crisis hubs and supported refugees and internally displaced people. Hunting organisations and hunters mobilised early thanks to their local knowledge, outdoor skills and experience with equipment and leadership. Civilian boating organisations have evacuated people, delivered supplies and maintained vital transport when roads and bridges were destroyed.

Together with key figures in Sweden's civil defence and representatives of the Swedish outdoor movement, we discuss how outdoor recreation can contribute to preparedness efforts.

content.title: After the first week – what happens next?
content.description: In a crisis, society's help will first go to those who need it most. Authorities recommend that households manage on their own for at least a week. This requires stable structures, responsibilities and resources, and a civil society that not only wants to contribute but is part of the solution.
content.extendedDescription:
The authorities are now clear: all households should be able to manage on their own for at least a week in a crisis or war, because society's resources will first be directed to the most vulnerable. But what happens after that week? Are society's resources sufficient, and how do we integrate outdoor organisations into Sweden's total defence?

Current analyses show that civil society is crucial to Sweden's ability to manage crises and war. This is evident both in Myndigheten för civilt försvar's civil society forum and in experiences from Ukraine, where voluntary organisations became essential societal actors.

Together with key figures in Sweden's total defence and representatives of the Swedish outdoor movement, we discuss how outdoor organisations can become part of Sweden's preparedness efforts.

content.title: As fears of crisis and war grow, mental ill health increases: outdoor recreation as a key to public health
content.description: Sweden faces its most serious security situation since the Second World War. The increased threat affects not only critical infrastructure and preparedness but also people's mental health profoundly. Psychological preparedness is a crucial component of total defence.
content.extendedDescription:
Research and experience show that prolonged worry, uncertainty and threats create psychological stress across the population. According to the WHO's latest needs assessment in Ukraine, 46 per cent of the population reports mental health problems after three years of full-scale war. Experience from the pandemic also shows how powerfully outdoor recreation can act as a protective factor during crises: nature became one of the most important sources of recovery, stability and reduced anxiety.

Sweden has a strength few countries possess: an outdoor recreation movement of 7,000 associations with two million memberships. Research shows that nature and outdoor recreation reduce stress and anxiety, among other benefits, and strengthen recovery.

These psychological mechanisms can also protect populations during crises and war. How can society make use of this movement's strength and the lessons from the pandemic about the importance of outdoor recreation?

content.title: Trump's new pharmaceutical policy – does Sweden have a plan as the rules change?
content.description: Trump's MFN pharmaceutical policy is shaking Europe. content.extendedDescription:
The pharmaceutical industry is one of Sweden's most important foundational industries, crucial for growth, healthcare productivity and national resilience. Meanwhile, the playing field is changing rapidly.

China is sharply increasing investment, and the United States' Most Favored Nations pricing policy has changed conditions for the global pharmaceutical industry and shaken Europe.

The consequences are already here. European research and production initiatives are being paused or relocated, investment is failing to materialise, and new medicines are not being launched or are being withdrawn in countries with heavy price pressure.

Sweden is particularly vulnerable. We have low prices, low uptake of new medicines and a model that does not fully value innovation's societal benefits. This makes us less attractive for investment, research and launches.

What is now needed to secure patients' access to new medicines and strengthen growth, resilience and Sweden's position as a leading life science nation?

Is there a plan now that the rules have changed?

content.title: How can tax rules promote reuse in the property sector?
content.description: Reuse and circular construction are central to the climate transition, but current tax and VAT systems often work against them. How do tax rules affect property owners' incentives, and how can they change to encourage sustainable investment?
content.extendedDescription:
From an income tax perspective, rules on deductions for scrapped assets limit opportunities for reuse. If parts of a building are retained, the owner must continue depreciating tax values no longer recognised in the accounts. Changing the rules would improve cash flow and release capital for sustainability measures.

VAT also creates obstacles. Valuing reused building components is often complex, potentially resulting in output VAT without a corresponding deduction entitlement. For stakeholders with limited deduction rights, reuse therefore becomes an actual cost.

Property tax compounds the problem. Investment in environmental and energy improvements can raise the assessed value and thus the ongoing tax burden.

The consequences are clear: current tax rules can effectively favour demolition over reuse.
The seminar discusses the measures needed to make reuse the obvious choice.
content.subject: Construction
speakerTitles: Nordic & Europe Central Tax & Law Sustainability Leader

content.title: How do we measure sustainable business beyond growth?
content.description: Our economic system still rewards what can be counted in money – not always what truly counts. As long as business success is measured in growth, both people and the planet risk becoming expendable resources. But what if growth is no longer the goal?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar challenges the metrics guiding today's business decisions and the idea that more is always better. Starting from concepts such as degrowth, decoupling and true cost, we explore what happens when the economy must operate within planetary and social boundaries.

What happens if success is measured in impact or resilience rather than revenue? In actual benefit rather than volume? In lives saved, calories produced per unit of energy used, actual equality or perceived fairness – rather than growth?

What do new goals and KPIs look like in practice? Efficiency measures aligned with planetary boundaries, absolute resource limits following the logic of CSRD – or entirely new ways to measure value creation?

Are today's standardised ESRS sufficient, or are tailored measures needed for an economy that can no longer afford to grow at the expense of its own future?

This is a discussion for anyone who suspects that the sustainable transition is failing not for lack of ambition, but because we are still measuring the wrong things.

content.title: How to win tomorrow's energy customer
content.description: The energy market is changing rapidly while customer expectations rise. What happens when the energy sector stops complicating things and starts truly listening to customers? How can it become genuinely customer-centred and strengthen competitiveness?
content.extendedDescription:
Today, customers expect energy companies not only to supply electricity but also to help them understand and manage energy issues. Yet the industry remains stuck in a technology-led mindset that does not fully match customers' actual needs.

The seminar features two energy companies representing both transformation and innovation: international energy company E.ON, on a journey towards stronger customer focus, and new company Buddy Energy, which has built its offering around customer needs from the outset.

Together, we discuss what energy customers actually want, share insights from EY's industry survey and explore how energy companies can change to create customer value in an increasingly complex market.

content.title: How well prepared are we to handle sabotage against our drinking water supply?
content.description: Cooperation between organisations to improve understanding of their different roles, identify needs and develop shared ways of working during suspected incidents can be crucial when essential services are sabotaged. Robust preparedness is a vital part of strengthening civil defence.
content.extendedDescription:
When drinking water is threatened: Sweden's first joint sabotage exercise involving water and wastewater operations and the police.

This seminar highlights experience from a completed field exercise. Water and wastewater staff from Region Gotland and the Gotland local police area, supported by Livsmedelsverket, jointly practised a realistic sabotage scenario involving a municipal drinking water facility. The exercise clearly demonstrated the value of cooperation between organisations in improving understanding of roles, identifying needs and developing shared ways of working during suspected incidents. Particular emphasis is placed on the value of field exercises and planning for success. Robust water and wastewater preparedness is a vital part of strengthening civil defence.

content.title: Avtal 27 – does the Industrial Agreement deliver when the world is in turmoil?
content.description: Ahead of Avtal 27, the Swedish model is in focus. In a time of economic uncertainty and geopolitical turmoil, the Industrial Agreement's ability to deliver competitiveness, long-term stability and good wage growth is being tested. How can we jointly ensure that Sweden's collective bargaining model holds firm in an unstable world?
content.extendedDescription:
For almost three decades, the Industrial Agreement has laid the foundations for stable wage formation and stronger competitiveness in Sweden. The wage benchmark set by industry has provided predictability for businesses and employees and contributed to a well-functioning labour market. Ahead of Avtal 27, the social partners are once again coming together to shape the conditions for the coming years.

Meanwhile, the Swedish economy is undergoing a transition. Geopolitical turmoil, technological development, climate investments and new global conditions affect industry and, consequently, the entire labour market. This calls for responsibility, a long-term approach and the ability to cooperate.

This seminar brings together representatives of trade unions, employers and businesses to discuss how the Industrial Agreement can continue to contribute to stability, competitiveness and good conditions in a changing world. The discussion focuses on the choices ahead of Avtal 27 and the continued development of Sweden's labour market model.

content.title: The future of bus services — how do we ensure sustainable procurement in public transport?
content.description: Contracted public bus services underpin many people's daily lives and businesses' skills supply and are essential to Sweden meeting its climate targets. But the system now faces a crisis: several operators are making losses. What is needed to reverse the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish bus companies operate in a pressured market with declining profitability, greater uncertainty and increasing regulatory demands. Previously stable conditions have been replaced by volatility, rising costs and higher risks.

Current contract models are identified as a central problem, with an uneven division of risk between contracting authorities and bus companies. Technical and regulatory demands are increasing while capital costs rise, particularly for vehicles. The result is wider variation in bid prices, with risk appetite carrying increasing weight. In the long run, competition is threatened as fewer operators participate in procurement under these conditions.

A new report from Sveriges Bussföretag analyses market conditions and risk allocation in publicly procured bus services and how they affect companies' ability to operate sustainably over the long term with passengers at the centre.

content.title: Coastguard operations: key to total defence, but without the right conditions?

As its mission has expanded, demands on its operations have grown, while resources and staffing have not fully kept pace.

This seminar brings together representatives of the authority, politics and trade unions to discuss Kustbevakningen's role in total defence and what is needed to ensure its long-term functioning.

content.title: The limit has been reached! Provide more resources so customs officers can stop more drugs and weapons at the border
content.description: Organised crime is growing, and large quantities of drugs, weapons and illegal goods are crossing Sweden's borders. More tools are being provided, but are there enough resources?
content.extendedDescription:
Tullverket is getting more tools, but have resources kept pace? Serious organised crime poses a grave threat to society. Criminal networks are well organised and well resourced. They operate across national borders, resulting in large flows of drugs, weapons and money.
Tullverket plays a central role in stopping these flows. In recent years, the agency has gained expanded powers and more tools to combat the criminal economy. At the same time, pressure on its operations is increasing, particularly in operational work at the border. In 2025, customs seized 10 tonnes of drugs.
Staffing needs to grow in line with the agency's remit, but reinforcements have not fully kept pace with it.
What might officers encounter in the field? What is being said in the corridors of power, and what does Tullverket's management say?
How do these developments affect the ability to recruit, retain and develop the right skills among the staff who, in practice, determine whether border controls work?
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: From talking about young people to building with them: how can young people participate and influence in practice?
content.description: Segregation, insecurity, crime and mental ill-health are major challenges in disadvantaged areas. Yet young people's participation often remains mere words, without structures enabling action and real influence. Building with young people strengthens democracy and prevention.
content.extendedDescription:
A discussion-based seminar with refreshments. Young people's participation and influence are often mentioned but rarely put into practice. How do we move from words to action, from talking about young people to building with them?
We share how, together with young people, we have built social and inclusive infrastructure in local communities that increases their participation and influence. We show how this strengthens democracy and participation in society while preventing challenges such as segregation, crime and mental ill-health.
Young people in disadvantaged areas describe being talked about often, but rarely talked with. The conversation focuses on designing initiatives that give young people not only a voice but also real influence and the ability to act in preventive work. Hear their journeys from participants to leaders and co-creators, and how they now make a difference for other children and young people.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: If war comes — will Sweden's digital backbone hold?
content.description: Communications, command, data and robust infrastructure are now integral to operational capability. As threats intensify, the question becomes urgent: will critical networks, communications links and digital dependencies hold when it really matters?
content.extendedDescription:
After decades of dismantling, responsibilities and cooperation must be rebuilt while pressure from the outside world increases. Can the public sector, Försvarsmakten and companies providing essential services move quickly enough to deliver real operational effect? Who takes responsibility when civilian and military dependencies meet in real time?

At the same time, fragmentation, short-term procurement and unclear responsibilities risk making the digital backbone a weak link. Capability is only as strong as its weakest procurement. How do we prevent governance, processes and decision-making pathways from becoming the bottleneck when the pace must increase?

But the issue is not just about withstanding the first disruption. How do we build a digital defence that can adapt, develop and endure? This requires the ability to repair, restore and strengthen critical systems while pressure continues.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: The suburbs, racism and the 2026 election — who gets to define the problems?
content.description: Ahead of the 2026 election, crime, safety and ‘vulnerable areas’ dominate political debate. Problems in the suburbs are often described in simplistic and stigmatising terms. How does this framing affect political priorities and legislation?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has recently faced sharp criticism in a UN report for shortcomings in its work against racism. The report criticises several political reforms, including the proposed good-conduct requirement and the introduction of so-called security zones. It warns of an increased risk of discriminatory racial profiling, growing exclusion and economic inequality. This panel discussion provides a platform for perspectives, experiences and analyses that are too rarely given space in public debate.

The event takes the form of a moderated panel discussion and addresses, among other things:
- How ‘vulnerable areas’ and crime are framed in the election debate ahead of 2026.
- Consequences for political priorities, legislation and democratic participation.
- Alternative perspectives and solutions that rarely receive space in national debate.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: The fragile goal – when building society requires both trust and control
content.description: During the spring, Sweden's church leaders met parliamentary party leaders to discuss trust and its breakdown. What happens to the goal when fear becomes the driving force rather than the vision? What does it say about society when the church's work becomes a political statement? What can politics and the church learn from each other?
content.extendedDescription: Archbishop Martin Modéus and church leader Karin Wiborn took part in the spring's discussions with party leaders, which covered migration, development aid, children's vulnerability and the new democracy requirements. Here, they meet Professor of Political Science Marie Demker and Aftonbladet editorial writer Susanna Kierkegaard in a panel discussion about trust and control, distrust and shifting values – concepts that recurred in the reflections after every party leader discussion. Do the churches have something to teach politics, and how can we help each other build a society in which we actually dare to trust one another?

content.title: Have we built too much bicycle parking in new housing?
content.description: Municipalities have increased bicycle parking requirements in new developments. But how should parking provision be sized now that new data on actual use is available? The issue is central to sustainable mobility, cost-effective construction and better use of space in properties.
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish municipalities have long used parking standards to encourage more sustainable travel and construction. As car parking requirements have been reduced, bicycle parking requirements have often increased. But how well do current requirements reflect actual use, and how should policy develop in light of new knowledge?
New data from 46 newly built housing projects provides a more evidence-based picture of how bicycle parking is used in practice. The results suggest that capacity and design should be based more on location, target groups and local conditions than on general standards. This raises important questions about how municipalities, developers and property owners can create solutions that both strengthen sustainable mobility and use space and resources more effectively.
The discussion explores how future requirements can become more relevant, efficient and evidence-based.

content.description: How do we create a county where people want to live and stay, with equal opportunities for a good life? Residents' needs do not follow our organisational boundaries. content.extendedDescription:
In Jönköpings län, we are tackling this challenge together. Starting with the question ‘What is best for Esther?’, we are developing collaboration between the region, the county's 13 municipalities, Jönköping University, Länsstyrelsen and other stakeholders. Through initiatives such as the senior leadership programme, we are strengthening leadership that takes responsibility for the whole. Municipal dialogues and new ways of working provide insights that we put into practice while learning along the way.

Welcome to a discussion about how we can strengthen our ability to collaborate and develop as one system – and realise the ambition of supporting a good life for everyone.

content.description: At a time often dominated by social challenges and crisis headlines, we also need to talk about bright spots and the forces driving us forward. The documentary Framtiden bor hos oss portrays precisely this: the irrepressible desire to create something of your own and take control of your own future.
content.extendedDescription:
We screen the documentary "Framtiden bor hos oss", in which journalist Jan Scherman and Khalid Mohammed visit suburban neighbourhoods in Göteborg to give us that very picture: everyday life behind the headlines. Join us beyond the news reports and discouraging headlines. The screening is followed by a conversation with some of the film's participants, focusing on these questions:
Young people's motivations: what makes young people dare to commit, break new ground and create change where others see obstacles?
Entrepreneurship as a tool: how can entrepreneurship and creating something of your own provide a way forward, not only for the individual but for the entire local community? Real confidence in the future: how can we, as a society and as decision-makers, best build an environment where young people feel hope, empowerment and the ability to act? This session is for anyone looking for energy, new perspectives and practical insights from the next generation of changemakers. You can also attend just the conversation, which starts after the film at 15:15.

content.title: Gambling problems — how can society better protect individuals?
content.description: Gambling addiction is a growing problem. More people are becoming trapped in games designed to create strong feelings of reward. For many, this leads to financial and relationship difficulties, stress and mental ill health, despite gambling companies' legal responsibility to protect players.
content.extendedDescription:
When someone develops gambling problems, their brain, everyday life and relationships are all affected. Many people seeking support have already accumulated large debts or lost contact with work and education. Society offers protection through gambling legislation, healthcare responsibilities and social services support, but efforts are not always coordinated or sufficient.

The seminar brings together researchers, healthcare professionals, public authorities and politicians to provide a clear picture of today's situation. They explain what research says about why gambling addiction develops, which forms of support work best and which parts of the current system need strengthening.

Together, we identify what must change for more people to receive help in time and how society can provide stronger protection for people at risk of gambling addiction.
content.subject: Research
speakerTitles: Chair of the Primary Care Committee's Public Health and Dental Care Subcommittee

content.title: Water, wastewater and climate adaptation – how long can decisions be postponed?
content.description: Sweden talks increasingly about robustness. Yet much of its water and sewer network is ageing and was built for a different climate. Government inquiries on greater climate adaptation have clarified both investment needs and systemic risks. Political decisions are still missing.
content.extendedDescription:
Government inquiries into greater water and wastewater preparedness and climate adaptation have clarified investment needs and systemic risks. Yet the key issues of responsibility and funding have still not been advanced politically. Meanwhile, pressure is growing. Cloudbursts and floods strain municipalities and insurance systems. Drinking water supplies and stormwater management are increasingly strategic issues. Every year without decisions increases the investment backlog and vulnerability.

Most funding currently comes from municipal water and wastewater charges. Is it reasonable for households and property owners alone to bear the costs of climate adaptation and robustness? Does Sweden need a national recovery plan for water and wastewater systems as part of a broader strategy for climate adaptation and societal preparedness?

content.title: Hybrid threats — from election interference to sabotage
content.description: Hybrid threats target the whole of society, regardless of sector. This means we all have a responsibility to detect, report and respond to them. How can hybrid threats affect our society, and how do we counter them?
content.extendedDescription:
Hybrid threats challenge the boundaries between war and peace, civilian and military, national and international. They can range from interference with democratic processes, disinformation and cyberattacks to sabotage of critical infrastructure and space-based systems.

The threats target the whole of society, regardless of sector. This means we all have a responsibility to detect, report and respond to hybrid threats. But not everything can be threatening — how should we approach such a diffuse threat landscape?

In this seminar, we follow a connected scenario from election interference to state-funded terrorism and sabotage. A panel discusses solutions for countering hybrid threats in Sweden. Among other things, a recently developed toolkit to help civilian authorities with this important work will be presented. How can different organisations act, and what does ‘managing’ hybrid threats mean?

content.title: The future of district heating – which bioenergy should be used?
content.description: District heating is central to the energy system – but which bioenergy will be sufficient in future?
content.extendedDescription:
District heating plays an important role in Sweden's energy system and the transition towards a more robust, electrified society. It provides half of heating and a tenth of electricity generation. Meanwhile, the sector faces crucial questions about long-term competitiveness and access to sustainable bioenergy.
Demand for forest raw materials is growing from several directions, particularly forestry and chemicals industries, while new EU regulations and national interpretations affect which fuels are feasible and profitable. Energimyndigheten's scenarios also indicate changing conditions for both bioenergy and district heating's future role.
How do we secure a sustainable long-term bioenergy supply? What is the relationship between the energy sector and the forest industry?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: From strategy to reality – how can innovations make a real difference for patients?
content.description: Sweden has major regional differences in access to new cardiovascular and cancer treatments. Despite national strategies, patients do not gain equitable access to innovative treatments quickly enough. How can we create clearer responsibility, better coordination and faster implementation nationwide?
content.extendedDescription:
Cardiovascular disease and cancer are Sweden's two largest major diseases and cause the most deaths. Despite significant medical advances, new treatments reach patients at different speeds depending on where they live. During the discussion, patient representatives question politicians directly to highlight the consequences of today's inequalities and opportunities for improvement. We explore how Sweden can establish clearer responsibilities, better coordination and more effective processes for introducing innovative medicines. What decisions are needed to turn strategies and action plans into reality for patients? And how does the panel intend to pursue the issue after the election?

Networking in the garden follows the panel discussion. The event is organised by Riksförbundet HjärtLung, Nätverket mot Cancer and Amgen. It is open to everyone, with no advance registration required. Welcome!

content.title: Do not ban fishing for household consumption – our oldest form of fishing carries culture into the future
content.description: Coastal communities have fished for their own households for thousands of years. This fishing is sustainable and has never threatened fish stocks. Yet the proposed new fisheries law would ban all net fishing for household consumption in Swedish waters, a proposal we hope never becomes reality.
content.extendedDescription:
Gotlands Husbehovsfiskeförening and Kullens Fiskareförening invite you to a discussion about our oldest and gentlest form of fishing: fishing for household consumption. It has existed as long as people have lived by the sea, threatens no stocks and destroys neither seas nor seabeds. It is sustainable, contributes to thriving fishing villages and carries valuable cultural heritage into the future. It is also an important resource for strong food preparedness.
Come and hear the arguments against a ban, learn more about small-scale fishing, ask questions and meet some of its strongest advocates.
Welcome to our meeting place: fishing for household consumption – an important carrier of culture and essential to food supplies in a crisis.
content.subject: Culture

content.title: Concern as a driving force for a green future
content.description:
The climate crisis threatens our future – emissions are increasing when they should be falling rapidly.
Are you worried about children's future too? You are not alone! It is easy to feel powerless in the face of inadequate climate policy. How can we create a future to look forward to?
content.extendedDescription:
We talk about targets, prices at the pump and roadmaps. But something else is simmering beneath the surface: worry, anger, grief – and a growing sense of betrayal. A lack of will is not the problem: 89% of the world's population wants strong climate policy. A lack of knowledge is not the problem. What is missing is courage.

Parents know that the climate crisis concerns their children's future. Yet people continue to accept short-term thinking, denial and political games – as if time were infinite.

Rebellmammorna and Rebellpapporna say enough is enough and are creating a space in Almedalen that otherwise does not exist:
• For anger at how slowly things are moving.
• For fear about what we are losing.
• For the will to bring about real change.

When emotions are given space, they have the potential to become a powerful force.
We invite you to a conversation where the audience interacts and provides input for discussion with our panellists. This is a space where every voice is heard and every voice is needed. We have no time for more comfortable conversations.

content.title: Young people's views on sport
content.description: Sport is often highlighted as a positive force in society, but far from all young people feel included. What do they really think about sport and club activities?
content.extendedDescription:
Today, the sports movement is an integral part of many people's lives, contributing to community, health and civic engagement. At the same time, a substantial proportion of young people are wholly or partly outside organised sport. There are many reasons, and the picture is more complex than public debate often suggests.
To better understand young people's views on sport, Svenska Friidrottsförbundet, together with Ungdomsbarometern, has conducted studies examining their attitudes, motivations and perceived barriers. The findings both confirm existing knowledge and offer new perspectives on how the sports movement is perceived today.
During this Almedalsveckan seminar, we present the studies' key conclusions in a lecture, followed by a panel discussion. Together, we discuss how sport and the enjoyment of physical activity can become more relevant, inclusive and appealing to more young people, based entirely on their own motivations and wishes.

content.title: Swedish Middle East policy 1948–2026
content.description: Israel and the Middle East are constantly in focus in Swedish politics. But how has Swedish policy developed and changed since Israel was established in 1948? Where do the political parties stand today?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's relations with Israel and the Palestinians have shaped our foreign policy for over seven decades and remain among our most debated issues. But what happened behind closed doors from 1948 to 2026 has never been told. Until now.

In the book ‘From Stockholm to Jerusalem: The Untold History of Sweden's Middle East Policy’ by Daniel Schatz, PhD, fifteen Swedish, Israeli and Palestinian heads of government and foreign ministers, along with around eighty ambassadors and senior politicians, share their experiences and reveal what actually happened behind the scenes.

This is followed by a panel with political party representatives. It will be a very engaging seminar and discussion! Based on 15 years of research, previously classified archive material and over a hundred in-depth interviews.

content.title: The role of buildings in a future energy system?
content.description: The building stock is an important part of the energy system, but its role is changing. How do major ongoing shifts such as demographic change, electrification, battery technology and EU emissions policy affect Swedish property owners' role in the system?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden is currently implementing the EU's EPBD (Energy Performance in Buildings Directive), which aims to make the building stock more energy-efficient and, eventually, emission-free. At the same time, rapid changes in the surrounding energy system will have a tangible impact in the coming years. Plug-in vehicles are on the verge of dominating the vehicle fleet, and developments in battery chemistries and bidirectional charging could take their role several steps further. Sweden's electricity surplus is attracting well-capitalised data centre operators, further spurred by major AI company stock market listings this summer, and electricity market conditions could change quickly. What overall picture does this paint of the role of buildings and property owners in the new energy system? How does our built environment need to respond and contribute?

content.title: From strategy to results – how can Sweden strengthen its position as a life science nation?
content.description: Life science is a Swedish strength, but the system is fragmented and implementation of the life science strategy is insufficient. Long-term investment, clearer priorities, coordination and implementation capacity are needed to secure Sweden's position as a leading life science nation.
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish life science policy needs to step up to realise the full potential of one of our most important future industries. The national strategy has been updated, but implementation remains insufficient. Responsibilities are unclear, and there is a lack of long-term investment, shared priorities, action plans with timelines and resources, structured follow-up, problem-solving capacity and the ability to drive forceful, coordinated change. Meanwhile, other countries are making long-term, coordinated investments in this field.

For Sweden to retain its position as a successful, competitive life science nation, clearer direction, greater mobilisation and stronger implementation are required.

In the seminar, politicians, healthcare, academia and business discuss who takes responsibility for driving work forward and which models best strengthen governance, coordination and implementation to move Swedish life science from strategy to results.

content.title: Values-led urban development – good neighbours as a source of societal benefit
content.description: How can we create a society with a natural place for everyone through healthcare, social care and education? What happens when values guide and underpin urban development, and when a district must accommodate 10,000 residents?
content.extendedDescription: When fully developed, Stora Sköndal will be a district where 10,000 people live, work, study and lead their lives. Its considerable natural and cultural assets provide a place accommodating different needs, focusing on inclusion, diversity and sustainability – a society with room for everyone. Urban development faces complex sustainability challenges requiring a balance between social, environmental and economic perspectives. Socially, inclusive and safe environments are needed, but segregation and inequality risk worsening without long-term planning. Society has many positive forces and initiatives, and successful cooperation makes us stronger. Environmentally, cities must reduce climate impact through energy efficiency, sustainable transport and ecosystem preservation, while urbanisation increases pressure on land and resources. Economically, major investments and affordable housing are needed, creating tensions between profitability and social sustainability.
